articles.title: Caso Master: pai de Vorcaro apresenta ao presidente do STF novo pedido de liberdade | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa de Henrique Vorcaro anexou laudo médico sobre quadro de diverticulite aguda e alegou descumprimento do prazo legal de 90 dias para revisão da prisão preventiva.
articles.summary: Defesa de Henrique Vorcaro anexou laudo médico sobre quadro de diverticulite aguda e alegou descumprimento do prazo legal de 90 dias para revisão da prisão preventiva.
articles.body:
A defesa de Henrique Vorcaro , pai do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, apresentou nesta terça-feira (3) um novo pedido de liberdade ao Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ). Caberá ao presidente da Corte, Luiz Edson Fachin , analisar o caso.

Os advogados solicitam a revogação da prisão preventiva ou a concessão de prisão domiciliar em razão do estado de saúde.

Henrique Vorcaro foi preso em 14 de maio de 2026, sob suspeita de integrar o suposto núcleo de coerção e intimidação ligado às investigações do caso Master. Ele está detido há mais de 170 dias.

No pedido encaminhado à Corte, a defesa anexou um relatório médico emitido em 28 de outubro de 2026. O laudo aponta episódios recorrentes de diverticulite aguda, com registro de internações hospitalares e crises.

O documento também diz que Henrique Vorcaro possui indicação para a realização de cirurgia no cólon.

Diante desse cenário, os advogados afirmam que o quadro clínico se encaixa nas hipóteses previstas em lei de conversão da prisão preventiva em domiciliar.

Além da questão médica, os defensores afirmam que não está sendo observada a obrigação legal de revisão da necessidade da prisão preventiva a cada 90 dias.

A prisão de Henrique Vorcaro ocorreu durante desdobramentos de investigações que apuram supostos crimes de intimidação, obtenção de informações sigilosas e invasões a sistemas informáticos.

Essas ações teriam sido realizadas pelo grupo "A Turma", investigado na Operação Compliance Zero. Henrique Vorcaro teria ficado responsável pelo financiamento do grupo após a prisão do filho.

Em setembro, a defesa já havia acionado a presidência do STF argumentando demora e questionando a competência da Corte para conduzir os atos referentes ao pai do empresário, sustentando que ele não possui foro por prerrogativa de função.

O presidente do STF, Luiz Edson Fachin, reuniu no seu gabinete os inquéritos sobre o caso.

articles.title: Lula e política econômica: aliados pedem defesa do equilíbrio fiscal | G1
articles.standfirst: Ideia de aliados é que o presidente acalme o mercado, fale sobre a necessidade de equilíbrio das contas públicas e descarte 'mágica' na economia em seu novo mandato.
articles.summary: Lula e política econômica: aliados defendem que o presidente garanta o equilíbrio fiscal e afaste rumores de mudanças drásticas para acalmar investidores.
articles.body:
Depois de ruídos no último fim de semana, sobre sugestões de mudanças na política econômica, aliados do presidente Lula defendem que ele use o prometido pronunciamento desta semana sobre a vitória nas urnas para garantir o equilíbrio fiscal em seu quarto mandato e afastar qualquer "mágica" na área econômica.

A avaliação é que a palavra para acalmar investidores deve vir do próprio presidente da República, reeleito para um novo mandato à frente do Palácio do Planalto.

No fim de semana, circulou a informação de que Lula poderia receber para uma conversa André Lara Resende, um dos pais do Plano Real, para avaliar uma ideia do economista de redução da taxa de juros a até 7,5% ao ano, para depois fixar um teto tanto para a inflação como para a taxa Selic do Banco Central.

A ideia foi refutada pelo ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, que negou que o encontro do presidente com o Lara Resende aconteceria e garantiu que não haveria mudanças na política econômica.

Próximo de André Lara Resende, Aloizio Mercadante foi apontado como responsável por fazer a mediação do encontro entre Lula e o economista.

Mercadante, que preside o Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social ( BNDES ), também disse, no fim de semana, que não havia nada marcado para um encontro entre os dois para os próximos dias.

Dario Durigan tem afirmado que vai apresentar, em breve, medidas ao presidente Lula para garantir o cumprimento do centro da meta fiscal do próximo ano, que é de superávit de 0,5% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB).

A ideia é fazer um ajuste fiscal durante os próximos quatro anos para evitar um corte drástico de gastos, que poderia comprometer programas sociais.

O presidente Lula, por sinal, veio a público, pelas redes sociais, para garantir que seu governo não iria cortar nenhum programa social e que irá cumprir todas as promessas feitas durante a eleição.

Durante o período eleitoral, Lula aumentou o Bolsa Família e concedeu benefícios para os microempreendedores individuais.

Economistas que já trabalham com o presidente Lula lembram que seus dois primeiros mandatos foram um sucesso porque ele seguiu a receita de promover um ajuste fiscal, gerar superávits primários, o que garantiu queda da taxa de juros e crescimento elevado do país. Por outro lado, quando o PT decidiu testar uma nova política econômica, deu tudo errado.

A lembrança é da nova matriz de política econômica defendida pelo ex-ministro da Fazenda Guido Mantega durante o governo Dilma.

Na época, o Banco Central reduziu a taxa de juros para 7,25% ao ano, mas não fez um ajuste fiscal, pelo contrário, aumentou suas despesas.

O resultado foi muito negativo na economia, gerando recessão e desemprego elevado, o que acabou enfraquecendo Dilma Rousseff , que sofreu impeachment em 2016.

articles.title: Gilmar Mendes diz que comando do TSE deve agir como 'árbitro equidistante' | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro do STF afirmou que 'silêncios e hesitações não são neutros' e disse que colegiado do tribunal assegurou que disputa eleitoral transcorresse dentro das regras democráticas.
articles.summary: Ministro do STF afirmou que 'silêncios e hesitações não são neutros' e disse que colegiado do tribunal assegurou que disputa eleitoral transcorresse dentro das regras democráticas.
articles.body:
O ministro Gilmar Mendes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), afirmou nesta terça-feira (3) que quem está no comando do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) deve ter uma postura de “árbitro equidistante” e disse que “silêncios e hesitações não são neutros”.

A Corte Eleitoral é presidida pelo ministro Kassio Nunes Marques , também integrante do STF. Ele assumiu o comando do TSE neste ano para conduzir as eleições de 2026 e permanecerá na presidência até maio de 2027.

Na publicação feita no X, Gilmar Mendes não mencionou Kassio Nunes Marques nominalmente nem citou episódios específicos.

A declaração ocorre, no entanto, após uma eleição marcada por decisões envolvendo diferentes instâncias da Justiça no dia do segundo turno ( leia mais abaixo ).

Um dos episódios ocorreu no encerramento da votação, em 25 de outubro . As campanhas de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) fizeram pedidos para ampliar o horário de votação diante de relatos de problemas que dificultavam a chegada de eleitores às seções.

A campanha de Lula acionou tanto o TSE quanto o STF . Por volta das 17h, o ministro Cristiano Zanin, do Supremo, determinou a prorrogação da votação até as 19h. Como parte das seções já havia encerrado os trabalhos, a medida não pôde ser aplicada em todos os locais.

Às 17h49, Kassio Nunes Marques assinou um ofício orientando as seções que ainda estavam abertas a permanecer em funcionamento até as 19h. Posteriormente, Cristiano Zanin esclareceu que sua decisão deveria ser aplicada apenas aos locais em que as urnas ainda não tinham sido fechadas.

Ministro Gilmar Mendes — Foto: Victor Piemonte/STF

Na postagem desta terça, Gilmar Mendes afirmou que as eleições de 2026 demonstraram que “as instituições de Estado são maiores do que os membros que as ocupam” e creditou ao colegiado do TSE a condução da disputa dentro das regras democráticas.

O ministro ponderou, porém, que a institucionalidade “não deveria precisar ser resgatada a cada eleição”.

“De quem está na condução do órgão que organiza o pleito espera-se a postura de árbitro equidistante que a Constituição pressupõe”, escreveu.

Gilmar Mendes acrescentou que, na condução de órgãos de elevada importância, “silêncios e hesitações não são neutros”.

Segundo ele, essas posturas podem “abrir espaço para decisões contraditórias” e levar outras instâncias a atuar em questões que poderiam ter sido solucionadas anteriormente.

“Podem abrir espaço para decisões contraditórias, levar outras instâncias a suprir, pelas vias próprias, o que poderia ter sido resolvido desde a origem e servir de pretexto a quem insiste em atacar um sistema eleitoral íntegro e confiável”, escreveu.

O ministro ainda elogiou a atuação conjunta dos integrantes do TSE.

“Desta vez, a colegialidade cumpriu seu papel. A solidez do processo eleitoral, contudo, não pode depender apenas da força do colegiado.”

No balanço feito após a eleição, Kassio Nunes Marques afirmou que a Justiça Eleitoral havia conduzido o pleito com segurança e que as eleições transcorreram “dentro da mais absoluta normalidade”.

articles.title: When will we know who controls Congress? It could be a while
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The stakes in Tuesday's election — which party will control Congress — are crystal clear. But when that will be known is impossible to say.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The stakes in Tuesday's election — which party will control Congress — are crystal clear. But when that will be known is impossible to say.

The Associated Press will be calling races in all 435 House districts and the 35 Senate contests that are up for election this year.

Control of the House depends on which party reaches 218 seats. Currently, 219 members caucus with Republicans, just one more than the minimum needed for a majority when all seats are filled. There are two vacancies now.

The bar for the Senate is 51 seats for Democrats or 50 for Republicans, since Vice President JD Vance can cast a tiebreaking vote for his party. Republicans have a 53-47 edge in the Senate right now.

During the last midterm elections in 2022, the AP called control of the Senate four days after Election Day, while the House call was eight days after.

During the presidential cycle of 2024, there was a bigger gap between the two. Senate control was called the day after Election Day, with the House call coming eight days later.

Some states consistently take days to count all their ballots. California , the nation's most populous, has seen thousands of mail ballots dropped off on Election Day. In 2022 , half the state's votes were counted after Election Day.

Other states like Alaska and Maine , which have key Senate races this year, use ranked choice voting.

A candidate can win with more than 50% of votes in the first round, but if no one reaches that threshold then the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and their votes are redistributed to the voter's second choice. The process can significantly delay results.

The AP does not make projections and will only declare a winner when it's determined there is no scenario that would allow the trailing candidates to close the gap.

articles.title: Ex-Chicago FBI chief sues DOJ, claims he was ousted over failed anti-ICE prosecutions
articles.summary: The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out after being wrongly blamed for failed prosecutions against anti-ICE protesters in the city.
articles.body: The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out of his job after he said he was wrongly blamed for the failed prosecution of six people who protested against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Windy City, according to a lawsuit he filed on Monday. Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence, according to the lawsuit. He said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer. "I saw the writing on the wall," DePodesta told The Associated Press. DePodesta accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros, of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT Hours after the lawsuit was filed, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed "Broadview Six" case. "There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court," Perry wrote in the order. Federal prosecutors brought charges against roughly 30 protesters during the federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, but many of those charges have since been dropped or dismissed. DePodesta’s lawsuit alleges that Boutros faced pressure from the DOJ throughout the immigration crackdown to slap protesters with felony charges. "Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration," DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the complaint. Boutros often pressured assistant U.S. attorneys to press charges "before investigating the objective evidence," according to the lawsuit, which says he wanted felony charges when assistant U.S. attorneys "favored misdemeanors or no charges at all." Last October, Boutros charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, in connection with their actions during a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview. Grand jury transcripts later turned over to the court showed that grand jurors twice declined to indict the six people as prosecutors sought charges, according to The Associated Press. Boutros dropped all charges against the six people in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct. Boutros "repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington" that the failure was DePodesta's fault "to deflect attention from his own malfeasance," DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the lawsuit. DePodesta denied Boutros’ claims to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out of his job due to the "political pressure Boutros created," according to the suit. The complaint alleges Boutros told DOJ leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, "conspired to destroy" the case. In September, one of the prosecutors on the "Broadview Six" case abruptly resigned, writing in a resignation letter that Boutros had "scapegoated and publicly vilified" her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party moving forward. The former defendants have asked the judge to appoint a special counsel to probe possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further "fact-finding" about communications between Boutros’ office and DOJ leadership. Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax. Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028. Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations. Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions. California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions.

California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development.

The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET.

6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.

7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close.

The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.

9 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.

10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon.

11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California and Washington state, with the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon also closing.

Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET.

articles.title: 5 potential midterm Senate upsets
articles.summary: Senate races are tightening in the closing days of the midterm cycle, expanding the battleground map and fueling both parties’ dreams of game-changing pickups. articles.body:
Senate races are tightening in the closing days of the midterm cycle, expanding the battleground map and fueling both parties’ dreams of game-changing pickups.

A handful of tight Senate races are soaking up the spotlight: Ohio, Iowa and Kansas are toss-ups in the latest ratings from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s partner, while Texas, Maine and Alaska edged out of the coin-toss column as of Monday.

But there are more possible flips on the table for both parties as support consolidates in the homestretch. As of Monday, 15 states were in the “lean” or “likely” categories under DDHQ’s forecast, giving both parties a fighting chance in the fight for Senate control.

Here’s a look at five potential upsets that could offer Election Day surprises:

Republicans have found themselves on defense in South Carolina, scrambling to protect the Senate seat that the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) held for more than 20 years.

Lindsey Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), was appointed to fill the vacancy after his unexpected death earlier this year. With President Trump’s support, she jumped into the race for a full term and emerged from a tough primary runoff despite concerns about her lack of political experience.

Trump has since made more than one last-minute visit to the Palmetto State in what many see as a sign of GOP stress in the red stronghold.

South Carolina is “a little bit more of a reach for Democrats” than toss-up contests like Kansas, said Geoffrey Skelley, DDHQ’s chief elections analyst, “because of the racial polarization and voting patterns in South Carolina.”

Both DDHQ and Cook Political Report rate South Carolina’s Senate contest as “lean Republican.”

“This could be an early barometer for Democrats on election night — if it’s even within a few points, gale force winds could be forming for Republicans,” Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote in a preelection analysis, though she predicted the seat will ultimately remain “just out of reach for Democrats.”

Republicans dominate in Trump’s home state of Florida, but forecasters have softened the Senate contest from safe-red ratings to show a real chance for Democrats amid frustration with the status quo.

Sen. Ashley Moody (R), who was appointed to replace Secretary of State Marco Rubio , is polling ahead of Democrat Angie Nixon by single digits in a state that Trump won by 13 points last cycle.

The winner of Tuesday’s election will serve the last two years of Rubio’s term, which is up in 2028, and would need to run again in two years for a full term in the upper chamber.

Both DDHQ and Cook Political Report now rate Florida’s Senate fight as “likely Republican,” a step closer to “safe” red territory than South Carolina’s rating.

Nixon, who defeated Trump whistleblower Alex Vindman in an unexpected primary upset , “would be faring better” without her Democratic Socialists of America affiliation, Taylor noted.

But Florida’s race could also be impacted by changes in the Hispanic and Latino bloc , which makes up roughly a third of the Sunshine State’s population . The demographic moved toward Trump in 2024 but appears to be turning back to Democrats amid frustration with the economy and immigration under a GOP-controlled Washington.

Former Sen. John Sununu (R-N.H.) is running for his old seat in the Granite State and is considered a top recruit for Republicans hoping to claw back ground in blue territory.

His opponent, Rep. Chris Pappas (D), has pulled ahead since the primary, giving Democrats some breathing room — though the seat isn’t a lock for the party just yet.

In the run-up to the election, Pappas suggested his opponent was purposefully keeping his first name out of campaign materials to confuse voters into thinking that his brother, former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R), was the one on the ballot.

“Look, if people thought they were voting for me, my brother would be up by 30 points. Come on,” Chris Sununu said on CNN . John Sununu said his brother was “totally wrong.”

“This is a race that no one thought would be in play a year ago, and it’s a toss-up race right now,” the Republican candidate added.

Cook Political Report rates the New Hampshire Senate seat as “lean Democrat,” while DDHQ moves it a step further to the left, to “likely Democrat.”

With Pappas in position to take the seat, DDHQ also considers New Hampshire as the most likely state to see a split-ticket result for Senate and governor, with incumbent Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte on track to fend off Democrat Cinde Warmington.

Republicans could also have a shot in the open race to replace Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) in the upper chamber.

Smith is supporting Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who beat out centrist Rep. Angie Craig (D) in the primary, against former NFL reporter Michele Tafoya (R), who has distanced herself from Trump while sporting his endorsement.

Republicans have been hopeful that recent scrutiny on the state’s sprawling fraud scandal will open a door for them after Trump lost the state by single digits in each of his three elections.

Democrats, though, are trying to capitalize on economic woes and outcry over Trump’s immigration crackdown, which led to Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that roiled the state earlier this year.

Like New Hampshire, Cook Political Report rates the Minnesota Senate race as “lean Democrat” after moving it toward the GOP in late October, while DDHQ has it a step further to the left, at “likely Democrat.”

“While we still believe the national environment will lift Flanagan to victory, this race’s margin may ultimately even be closer than New Hampshire’s Senate contest, which has seen far heavier investment from outside groups on the airwaves,” Taylor wrote.

Mississippi could prove a sleeper race in the fight for the Senate majority.

Trump won Mississippi by more than 20 points in the presidential race, and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith started the cycle as the clear favorite.

But as the political winds shift toward Democrats across the country, closer-than-expected polling has raised concerns that Hyde-Smith, who ran behind Trump in 2020, could be in trouble. She’s also taken heat for an unartful response to rising beef prices, as she suggested there were “so many proteins to choose from.”

Democrats have rallied behind Scott Colom, the Lowndes County district attorney, and are pushing for support from Black voters to give him a boost in the Deep South.

Cook Political Report moved the race from “solid” to “likely” Republican in late October, noting that “a Democratic upset in Mississippi would signal a blue tsunami.” DDHQ also rates it “likely” Republican.

articles.title: PASTOR COREY BROOKS: El-Sayed's pitch to Black voters is the same old liberal condescension
articles.summary: Every day I work to lift up members of my community with American principles, and those in Michigan who vote for Abdul El-Sayed for are voting in the opposite direction.
articles.body: Like most Americans, I've been following the election, and Tuesday, Nov. 3, is the last day we can vote. I have to admit that from the South Side of Chicago, I've been watching the state near me, Michigan, with a heavy heart. On Tuesday, voters there will decide whether or not to send Abdul El-Sayed to the United States Senate. He is a progressive who wants to implement Medicare for All, and he wants to abolish ICE. He has Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in his corner (Britannica). What interests me about him is that he is part of a broader push on the left that sees American principles as the problem. El-Sayed says that he is not a socialist. He calls himself a capitalist, and the Democratic Socialists of America have never endorsed him. But one has to wonder if keeping that distance is part of his campaign strategy. Between 2017 and 2020, he spoke at six DSA chapter events and even gave the keynote speech at a 2019 fundraiser. The socialist organizers have called him "a longtime friend of Detroit DSA" (Fox News). In addition to this, 50 DSA members flew in from New York to knock on doors for him before the primary (Washington Examiner). I'll let Michigan decide what the most apt political label is for him. I'M DR. ABDUL EL-SAYED. THIS IS WHY I WANT MICHIGAN'S VOTE FOR SENATE He has made a concerted effort to show Black voters in the Detroit area that he is with them. He lost the city in the August primary, and since then he has visited Black churches, stood with Black pastors and put out an agenda for Black communities with housing timelines, minority business loans and school repairs. In September, he told a room full of female faith leaders in Detroit, "When it comes to Black communities in Michigan, when it comes to Black communities in America, there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down." It is important to notice the language here. He's talking to us as if we are people who are owed, as if our future depends on somebody else paying up. He sees us as members of the oppressed class, and he's trying to chill with us on that level, just like the good old White liberal used to do. I'M MIKE ROGERS. THIS IS WHY I WANT MICHIGAN'S VOTE FOR SENATE I've listened to him long enough to know that I can't find any of the things that I'd want to hear him say. He says nothing about embracing America without apology. Being an American means not relying on excuses, being responsible and taking accountability. But he says none of this. For 60 years, the left has talked to Black Americans this way, and I've seen the profound damage that kind of talk does in the communities that I serve. I have said this elsewhere. This socialism that candidates like El-Sayed lean heavily into is not a good thing. After all, we Black Americans were the first in America to truly live under the kind of government dependency that socialists now want for everyone. Though they were sold politically as programs that would lift us out of our history of oppression, the Great Society, the housing projects and welfare rules that punished marriage and work all trapped us in a vicious culture of dependency. EL-SAYED SCORES SINGLE-DAY FUNDRAISING RECORD AFTER HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES RIVAL In 1963, 23.6% of Black children were born to unmarried mothers. By 2023, the number had increased to 69%. Fathers were leaving, a check took the place of the man in the house, and marriage, faith and work started to look optional. Many Black Americans fled this life by using the American principles of uplift, and too many others found themselves in what has become known as the permanent Black underclass. That's what I see every day. I created Project H.O.O.D. to undo all of this damage with job training and character building, and by telling young people the truth, which is that government dependency doesn't have to be their destiny. DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS The people who rallied around El-Sayed have told us what they want. The DSA's 2026 program, "Workers Deserve More," has made the call for abolishing the Senate and the Electoral College and replacing the president and Supreme Court "with an executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress." They literally want to take down the greatest form of government ever devised. They have also talked about the need to "draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic." In 2021, a DSA convention resolution said that the United States "has never been and will never be a force for liberation." Amy Wilhelm, who sits on the DSA's National Political Committee, said, "The role of socialists ... is really to facilitate the defeat of our own nation." El-Sayed hasn't signed on to that program, and his own proposal is to end the filibuster. But these are the folks who walked his precincts, drumming up votes, and I'm pretty certain they'll want something for it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION A big part of why El-Sayed has advanced so far is White guilt. For a lot of White progressives, voting for a man like El-Sayed is a way to prove they're on the right side of race. They feel good backing a candidate who talks about debts owed to Black communities. It validates their social justice bona fides, and Black Detroit is left with the dependency. You can see the decay everywhere, and nobody stops to ask if more of the same socialist policies are working. The point here is not true Black uplift, but the innocence of White people, and El-Sayed is playing to that. El-Sayed has also used White guilt to protect himself. He has faced recent allegations that his family may have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. In 2012, his half-sister wrote online about "an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college." When he was asked about it, he said his family has no ties to the group and called the post "hearsay evidence from a tweet." Fact-checkers haven't found evidence that he himself has ties to the Brotherhood, and he has disavowed it. But when he went on "Meet the Press," he asked, "Why is this even a subject of debate?" When a voter at a town hall asked him to disavow the group, he said, "Sure, yeah, absolutely," and then went after the man: "You assume ... that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution." No reporter wants to be called an Islamophobe, just as nobody wants to be called a racist. It is the same fear that White guilt runs on, and he counts on that fear to make the question go away. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What all of this reveals is that there is nothing new about El-Sayed. Like the White liberal before him, he speaks to Black Americans as people who are owed, and he leans on the same socialist ideas that have already failed us. Every day I work to lift up members of my community with American principles, and those in Michigan who vote for Abdul El-Sayed are voting in the opposite direction. articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: The ghosts of 2006 are stirring — but will they catch the GOP?
articles.summary: A 2026 midterm analysis compares Trump's position to Bush's 2006 losses, weighing GDP growth, inflation and the Iran conflict against historical patterns.
articles.body: As the past is often prologue, much of the GOP is thinking today about the pounding the party took in 2006, the last time a Republican president led his party into the midterms for the second time. Older Republicans try not to let 1986 enter their heads. (The GOP lost eight Senate seats that year.) A truth bolt about polling from The Washington Post on Friday gave some hope to the mainstream, especially in states that voted for President Trump in 2024. The Post revealed that its pollsters had made 85,000 calls and sent 50,000 text messages in Kansas seeking to measure support for Senator Roger Marshall, who is being challenged by Democrat Adam Hamilton. While 32% of Kansas Democrats answered the calls and the texts from pollsters, only 12% of the GOP voters did. The Post conceded that these numbers provide "good reason to suspect the poll overestimates Democratic candidates’ support." THE SILENT MAJORITY PROBLEM AND WHY CAMPAIGN POLLSTERS KEEP 'FIGHTING THE LAST WAR' ON ELECTIONS That concession about the reality of polling in 2026 should give every analyst pause before citing "the polls." There isn’t great public data on which either party can rely, but there is history. For the GOP, the year most analogous to 2026 is 2006, and that’s scary. (The electorate is so different from 1986 that if it rhymes at all, it’s a reach.) In 2006, Republicans under President George W. Bush took a "thumpin’" — W’s term for the beat down of the GOP that year — so it is rational to consider the results from 20 years ago as a clear and present danger signal for Republicans. There are, however, some significant differences between this year and 2006, when the GOP lost a net six Senate seats and 30 House seats. FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS GDP in Q3 of 2006 was reported at just 1.6% in October of that year. (It was revised up to 2% later.) It is more than twice that this year, clocking in October at a very healthy 3.4%. Republicans can rightly point to an economy in rapid takeoff mode and voters feel that, especially the newly employed. Inflation in 2006 was at 2.1%, and it’s at 3.7% now. Gas was $2.25 a gallon then and $4.20 today. (National average in both cases.) Those numbers hurt the GOP candidates across the country. As do housing costs. In October 2006, the average U.S. interest rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was approximately 6.36%. It’s 7.25% today. Younger voters looking to buy their first home or "move-up" don’t know that the era of 3%-4% 30-year mortgage rates was an aberration. They just know they missed that window. The rational voter knows the hike in the cost of gas and the inflation is because President Trump is taking on the fanatics atop the Islamic Republic of Iran, our country’s sworn enemy of 47 years. Every president since Bill Clinton has warned the ayatollahs that force was on the table if it did not cease its nuclear program, which it has refused to do even after the one night of strikes that obliterated the program in 2025, the strike deemed "Operation Midnight Hammer." SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: A RED RETREAT FOR REPUBLICANS IS NOT THE SAME AS A BLUE WAVE IN 2026 But, the rogue regime didn’t get the message and immediately began rebuilding its shattered nuke program while continuing its support of terrorists around the region. Iran is responsible for the deaths of more than 1,000 Americans since the Islamic revolution of 1979, and is the greatest state sponsor of terror on the planet. If that regime can be cowed or collapsed, it will be President Trump’s greatest accomplishment. The biggest difference from 20 years ago, and one reason for Republicans to believe 2026 may not be a repeat of 2006? Twenty years ago, the U.S. had been at war for five years in Afghanistan and three in Iraq. October 2006 saw more than 100 U.S. military service memebrs killed in Iraq and 10 in Afghanistan. Contemporary reporting described it as one of the deadliest months of the war. The U.S. and its warriors and its military families were paying a very high price in 2006, and it did not seem that we were winning. The U.S. is decisively winning in the present conflict in Iran though it has not yet decisively won the battle. Only partisans of the left deny the blockade is bringing Iran to its knees. Twenty-three service members have paid the ultimate price since February. The cancer in the region for 47 years is being ripped out and the cost is high. Those are the statistical comparisons for two Republican presidents in their sixth year in office, though, of course, President Trump’s terms are non-consecutive. The good news for the GOP in the comparison is that President Bush’s second term got off to a terrible start in 2005 with the controversy over Terri Schiavo, Hurricane Katrina and the failed effort to reform Social Security. President Trump’s first 22 months back saw the wide open border shuttered and kept sealed, a massive tax hike averted, additional tax cuts made for tips and overtime and long overdue hikes in defense spending. Crime is down as the feds crack down and the war on police is over. DEI is DOA, and Dems continue to pursue policies considered extreme by the mainstream, including transgender craziness in sports for kids and objections to voter ID. Then there is "candidate quality" then and now. Democratic Senate winners in 2006 included James Webb (USMC war hero), a young Sherrod Brown in a still blue Ohio and John Tester, who was authentically Montana. MORNING GLORY: THE DEMOCRATS HAVE A 'FANATIC FOUR' OF EXTREMIST SENATE CANDIDATES This year they are running DSA’s Troy Jackson in Maine, extremist Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and scandal-plagued Mary Peltola in Alaska. Not sure what to call James Talarico, but he’s a very different candidate than, say, Bob Casey Jr., who beat Rick Santorum in Pennsylvania in 2006. (Sherrod Brown is 20 years older and trying a comeback from being fired by Ohio voters two years ago. Brown is looking and sounding like Joe Biden in 2022, and voters know it is a six-year term.) On the spending front: Total midterm spending was roughly $2.8 billion in 2006. The numbers are not in yet for this cycle, but the estimates are that approximately $4 billion will be spent and that the GOP has a significant advantage. President Bush made 16 campaign appearances in October 2006. President Trump hit 30 or more. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION GOPers should prep for another 2006, but should not be surprised if the results are not that bad. Senators Collins, Husted, Marshall and Sullivan have run great races. Challengers Mike Rogers in Michigan and Michele Tafoya in Minnesota are five-star candidates running against zero-star Ds. Redistricting is the last wrinkle. A "big blue wave" could wash out the gains the redistricting push brought, but then again, voters are much more aware of political issues today than ever before. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Trust the people" was Churchill’s phrase, which he got from his father. So we all should. Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: NBC News Exit Poll: How it works and how we use the results on election night
articles.summary: Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.
articles.body: Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices. An exit poll is a survey of voters taken as they leave (or exit) their voting location. Unlike public opinion polls ahead of elections that predict whether respondents will vote, exit polls capture the views of voters in person on Election Day. The exit poll also reflects the views of people who voted early or by mail — we take steps to reach those voters by phone and by mail, as well as online. Here’s how exit polls work, where they are conducted and how NBC News will be using the results on election night and in the days after. Who conducts the exit poll? For this year’s midterm election, exit polls are being conducted by SSRS, a survey and market research firm, on behalf of a group of news organizations: NBC News, ABC News, The Associated Press, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and MS NOW. The companies receive the same data, and NBC News then independently analyzes and reports on the exit poll results. What questions are asked? The national exit poll asks respondents whether they voted for the Democratic or Republican House candidate in their district, and in many states the poll also asks which candidates voters supported in Senate and governor’s races. In addition, the poll usually includes a number of questions about voters’ views, such as, “What is the most important issue facing the country?” The other key component of an exit poll is asking about voters’ demographics, such as age, gender, race and education level. These types of questions help illustrate how different groups of people voted and what mattered to them. Demographic data is also used to weight the exit poll — that is, to make sure the poll reflects the demographics of the electorate as well as the election results. The national and state exit polls include some different questions, to capture voters’ views on local issues and candidates. The news organizations jointly determine how the exit poll will be conducted and develop the questionnaire together. How are exit polls conducted? The in-person Election Day exit polls are surveys that voters in scientifically selected precincts are asked to fill out as they leave their polling place. The paper forms have about 25 questions. This year, interviewers will be stationed at over 450 polling locations in 15 Senate battleground states. Each interviewer follows local rules about where they can stand outside the polling location. The exit polls also include a pre-election survey to capture voters no matter how they participate, whether early, by mail or on Election Day. Before Election Day, respondents are surveyed through methods including mailed invitations, telephone and text interviews and online surveys. Interviewers then follow up with respondents to confirm that they voted and whom they ultimately voted for. Respondents can complete the poll in English or Spanish. On Election Day, interviewers count the people coming out after they have voted and are instructed to offer questionnaires to every third person or every fifth person, for example, from the time polls open until polls close. Interviewers phone in the results from the questionnaires to a data center three times during the day. Those results are tabulated with the pre-election survey results, and the exit poll is updated throughout the day as new data is collected. Are exit polls anonymous? Yes. In person, voters fill out the questionnaires themselves and deposit them in boxes, so their answers, like their actual ballots, are secret. Interviews conducted by mail, by phone and online do not retain any personal information about the voter who was interviewed. Which states will have exit polls? In addition to a national exit poll, which captures voters in all 50 states, there are also state exit polls this year in 45 states that have consequential Senate and governor’s contests. How many people are interviewed? The national exit poll sample will include over 75,000 voters at voting locations, online and by telephone. In 15 states, interviewers will be stationed outside at least 30 randomly sampled voting locations. In the remaining states, interviews are conducted via phone, online and mail. The sample size in each of these states will be about 4,000 voters: Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin. The sample size in Alaska will be about 3,000 voters, and it will also include interviews from voters at early-voting locations before Election Day. All other states with exit poll results for Senate and governor’s races will include between 500 and 3,000 voters. How do we use exit polls? The NBC News Decision Desk uses some exit poll data to help project race outcomes on election night, but the exit poll is primarily used to help tell the story of the election. The data gives viewers and readers real-time insight into what motivates voters and how they feel about the country. It’s the nation’s first look at who is turning out to vote this year and what is driving their choices. What does NBC News report and when? NBC News does not report any exit poll results before 5 p.m. ET on election night, and no exit poll results that may indicate the outcome of a race are reported until after all the polls are scheduled to close in that state. As election night goes on and interviewers on the ground call in more exit poll results, the data is updated and reweighted in real time.
authors: Stephanie Perry, NBC News Exit Poll Desk

articles.title: Three scenarios for how the US midterm results could unfold
articles.summary: Democratic wave or Republican resilience? Here are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.
articles.body:
After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.

According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.

In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.

Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in (which you can follow later on our results page ) and what it could mean for the country.

If history is any guide, midterm elections tend to favour the out-of-power party.

Add in what polls suggest is a historically unpopular president, a war with Iran that has driven up consumer costs and some controversial policies - like aggressive immigration enforcement and support for data centre construction - and you have the conditions for a so-called electoral wave.

In this first scenario, a huge wave is exactly what happens.

Democrats could not only take control of the House of Representatives but far surpass the 218 seats needed for a majority. They may win not only the dozen or so races that election analysts rate as too-close-to-call, they could also flip some seats in more solidly conservative terrain.

In the Senate, this scenario would require Democrats to win all or most of the current crop of races that are toss-ups, including some in traditionally conservative states. There would be at least one eye-popping victory in a place that hasn't elected a Democrat in a generation, Texas, or in nearly a century in the case of Kansas.

If this did happen, Democrats wouldn't just take control of the Senate, they would do so with a seat or two to spare. This might avoid any drama around a potential legal challenge by Republicans in Alaska where a judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans being on the ballot.

Democrats might accomplish this by boosting turnout of their voters and winning independent voters by sizable margins. This would reverse Trump's 2024 inroads with Hispanic voters and young men. Some Republican voters might also support the Democrats or just stay home.

This kind of a result would represent a stinging rebuke for Trump and his Republican Party, setting up two years of conflict between a newly invigorated Democratic Party with its hands firmly on the lever of legislative power and a president who seldom backs away from a fight.

If Democrats hold targeted House contests in Florida and win some Republican districts in North Carolina, Michigan, New York, Virginia and Kentucky. If they flip the Senate seat in South Carolina, it's going to be a good night for Democrats.

Maybe the polls won't be entirely wrong, but not entirely right either.

In this scenario, it could be that while they take enough of the low-hanging fruit in the US House contests to deliver a majority, it's not a sizable one.

This would mean Democratic leaders in the chamber would regularly have to wrangle with their fringe members on the left and the centre to ensure they have enough votes to pass legislation.

On the Senate side in this hypothetical, the Democrats would just flip a seat or two - North Carolina, for instance, seems all but assured - but the contests in the conservative heartland would prove to be out of reach.

Perhaps they're unable to unseat stubbornly resilient Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine or left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed can't keep Michigan in the Democratic column.

Maybe the duelling Dan Sullivans controversy is enough to sink Democratic candidate Mary Peltola in Alaska.

For this "Democratic trickle" scenario to unfold, the big Democratic turnout we've seen in early voting would be matched by a Republican surge on election day.

Trump's efforts to rally his base in Republican red states could help his party avoid the worst-case scenario. The races that were at or near the margin of error in polls might provide a mixed bag for both parties.

The result would be a divided Congress - and that's a recipe for political gridlock.

If Florida stays comfortably Republican across the board. If Democrats pick up some House seats in places like Virginia and Pennsylvania, but the Republican incumbents on more secure political ground across the country avoid getting washed away in a deluge.

This scenario involves Republicans resiliently holding on to both chambers of Congress.

For this to happen, the polls - which have previously underestimated Trump's support - need to be wrong and the toss-up races to mostly fall the way of Republicans.

Not only would Republican voters have to turn out in unexpectedly impressive numbers, independent and Hispanic voters who had seemingly soured on Trump's policies would have also to break his way in the end.

In this scenario, control of the House, far from being a done deal for Democrats, could end up coming down to California and its extended days-long counting process for mail-in ballots.

In the end, Republicans might eke out a slim overall majority thanks in part to efforts to draw more favourable congressional district lines in places like Texas, Florida and North Carolina.

It could also be that Republicans win all the Senate contests in the conservative states and they also flip Michigan, a seat that was held by Democrats heading into the vote.

Even if Republicans don't hold North Carolina or win in Democratic-controlled Minnesota or New Hampshire - races just on the periphery of competitiveness in this year's elections - they may at least make the Democratic candidates sweat.

If this was to happen, Trump might on Wednesday morning claim a renewed electoral mandate and push forward with his domestic and foreign policy agenda with the continued support of a Republican Congress.

If Senators Ashley Moody in Florida and Jon Husted in Ohio cruise to re-election. If Republicans hold their own in House races in Pennsylvania and Virginia, and they flip current Democratic seats in North Carolina, Ohio and Florida.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

articles.title: Which races might predict a 'blue wave'? Here's what to watch
articles.summary: The night's big question is whether a true wave will materialize for Democrats and how sizable it might be.
articles.body:
Americans are heading to the polls Tuesday in a historic set of midterm elections that will determine which party controls the chambers of Congress for the remainder of President Trump's time in office.

Democrats appear poised to make significant gains, with polling showing the party up between 7 and 11 points on the generic ballot . Republicans are braced for losses but hoping to hang on to Senate control.

The night's big question is whether a true wave will materialize for Democrats and how sizable it might be — how many U.S. House seats the party can flip, whether it can secure a Senate majority and whether Democrats take control of a majority of governorships.

The first polls close at 3 p.m. PST in parts of Kentucky and Indiana, and more Eastern states follow at 4 p.m. Here's a rundown of the possible outcomes and what to watch as Tuesday unfolds.

Blue House, red Senate: Democrats could win a House majority — either substantial or modest — while Republicans retain the Senate. Split control of Congress would give House Democrats the ability to launch investigations into the Trump administration and block Republican legislative priorities. Senate Republicans would be able to scuttle legislation coming out of the House and continue approving Cabinet and judicial appointments, including to any openings on the Supreme Court. Legislative gridlock — and possible government shutdowns — would be likely.

Blue House, red Senate: Democrats could win a House majority — either substantial or modest — while Republicans retain the Senate.

Split control of Congress would give House Democrats the ability to launch investigations into the Trump administration and block Republican legislative priorities. Senate Republicans would be able to scuttle legislation coming out of the House and continue approving Cabinet and judicial appointments, including to any openings on the Supreme Court. Legislative gridlock — and possible government shutdowns — would be likely.

Total Democratic control: A larger "blue wave" could occur, sweeping up House seats for Democrats and tipping key Senate races in their favor to hand Democrats a majority in both chambers. The Senate majority would likely be very narrow and could come down to a single race. Democrats would be able to block Senate confirmation of Cabinet and judicial appointments. They would be able to pass legislation, but Trump would hold veto power and the Democrats would be unlikely to secure veto-proof majorities on partisan priorities.

Total Democratic control: A larger "blue wave" could occur, sweeping up House seats for Democrats and tipping key Senate races in their favor to hand Democrats a majority in both chambers. The Senate majority would likely be very narrow and could come down to a single race.

Democrats would be able to block Senate confirmation of Cabinet and judicial appointments. They would be able to pass legislation, but Trump would hold veto power and the Democrats would be unlikely to secure veto-proof majorities on partisan priorities.

Wild cards: Most analysts agree there is very little chance that Republicans will keep House control. The potential for civic unrest looms over the election. If results in one or more races are contested by a losing party — as Trump and his allies have suggested is possible — the potential exists for prolonged uncertainty or a constitutional crisis.

Wild cards: Most analysts agree there is very little chance that Republicans will keep House control.

The potential for civic unrest looms over the election. If results in one or more races are contested by a losing party — as Trump and his allies have suggested is possible — the potential exists for prolonged uncertainty or a constitutional crisis.

The House majority could become clear before the night is over. The Senate majority could require a longer wait, particularly if it comes down to Alaska, which along with Hawaii is the last state to close polls, at 9 p.m. PST.

If the Democrats take the House, their full margin of victory likely won't be clear Tuesday night. Some key swing races are in states that have slower ballot counts, including California and Pennsylvania.

If a blue wave does not materialize and the race for the House majority narrows, how each party makes out could take longer to ascertain.

More than four dozen House races are competitive, including 18 that are considered tossups by election forecaster Cook Political Report . The additional 35 races are considered competitive but leaning towards one party. Whether additional, less competitive seats flip unexpectedly will be one indication of how much of a "wave" election this is.

Seven Senate seats are tossups : Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Three more are potentially competitive: South Carolina, which leans Republican, and Minnesota and New Hampshire, which lean Democratic under Cook's ratings.

North Carolina and Georgia, originally viewed as competitive seats, are now both seen by forecasters as fairly safe bets for Democrats.

The swing states could largely tip for Republicans or for Democrats, or the majority could come down to just a single race.

Experts say they're watching a handful of races that could provide early indicators for how the night may go, though predictions are always dicey and outliers are possible. Among the races to keep an eye on:

Kentucky's 6th: This Lexington-area U.S. House district has become an unexpected tossup, and with the nation's earliest poll-closing time, it could be a bellwether. "If Democrats win that district, then it's a Democratic tsunami," said Christopher Warshaw, a Georgetown University public policy professor. "Even if it's close, that would be pretty telling."

Iowa's 2nd: Forecasters have shifted this race to a tossup amid a difficult environment for state Republicans. If Republicans lose this seat — which belonged to Rep. Ashley Hinson, the party's Senate nominee — it could signal a blue wave on the bigger side.

New York's 17th: One of just three districts with a Republican incumbent that went blue in the 2024 presidential election, the outcome of this close race could "tell us a lot," said Todd Belt, a George Washington University political science professor.

Texas' 15th: This district offers a bellwether for Latino voters who moved right in 2024 but, signs indicate, may be shifting back to the left. The 34th and 35th districts in Texas could also be indicative.

Michigan Senate: If the Democrats lose Michigan, their path to Senate control becomes difficult. A win in Michigan is a best-case scenario for Republicans seeking to retain Senate control. Without Michigan, Democrats would have to flip five out of six swing seats in Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and South Carolina.

Maine Senate: If Democrat Troy Jackson wins in Maine, that will likely be a good sign for his party's chances at the Senate majority and their races in Michigan, Ohio and Iowa. Without it, Democrats could still take the majority, but Republicans' path will become easier.

Other states: If Democrats pull off wins in purple or red districts in Florida, Virginia and Pennsylvania, those could also signal a blue-leaning night.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Your hour-by-hour guide to 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: Election Day is here, and observers waiting with bated breath for results can expect a late night. Results will begin to trickle in at 6 p.m. EST, with control of Congress on the line. Although the final tabulation of votes could take days or even weeks, race projections Tuesday night will begin to paint a…
articles.body:
Election Day is here, and observers waiting with bated breath for results can expect a late night.

Results will begin to trickle in at 6 p.m. EST, with control of Congress on the line. Although the final tabulation of votes could take days or even weeks, race projections Tuesday night will begin to paint a picture of which party will clinch power on Capitol Hill.

Democrats need to win four GOP-held Senate seats and net three Republican House seats to flip either chamber. A later night would bode well for Republicans, particularly if key races are too close to call.

“If the polls are right, the generic ballot is relatively right, we’re going to be able to project pretty early in the night,” Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) chief election analyst Geoffrey Skelley told The Hill.

Here’s what to expect every hour as the polls close Tuesday:

Kentucky and Indiana will be the first states to have some of their polls close at 6 p.m., with their remaining polls closing at 7 p.m.

Skelley wrote in an October blog post that within the first two or so hours, results reported from the eastern part of the U.S. “will drive our initial understanding of what’s happening in the midterms.”

A flip in Kentucky’s 6th District could be indicative of a “big blue wave,” Skelley said. DDHQ rates the race between Republican Ralph Alvarado and Democrat Zach Dembo for outgoing Rep. Andy Barr’s (R) seat as a toss-up.

Polls close at 7 p.m. in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia and most of Florida and New Hampshire, though remaining polls in those last two states close at 8 p.m. West Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina’s polls close at 7:30 p.m.

Skelley noted that the elections in eight of these states — Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Virginia — will be “especially revealing” once polls close. Nearly 50 House races in these states are “at least mildly competitive — that is, not ‘safe’ for one party.”

The state with the quickest reporting in the country is Florida, with early data points expected to be available after closing. The Panhandle closes at 8 p.m.

Poll closings by 7:30 p.m. could show signs that a “blue wave” is coming, particularly if Democrats claim victories in Florida, Indiana, Georgia, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia.

“An actual Democratic win in any of these seats would be an electoral earthquake that all but guarantees a Democratic majority,” Skelley estimated. “Republican holds, meanwhile, would only mildly improve the GOP’s majority chances.”

Skelley told The Hill that after the fallout from Florida’s election results in 2000, its voting system became “the best in the country” and could map out what shakes out between 7:20 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.

“We’ll be able to make projections because we’ll be like, ‘Well, there’s no way someone’s ever coming that lead, or what have you,'” he said. “A lot of key districts, and a lot of Republican leading districts on paper, because of the Florida redraw –– Democrats are winning in those places. That will be like, well, it’s going to be real hard for Republicans to win if they’re losing in Florida like this.”

He emphasized that Florida is a “mixed bag” for both parties, so results between this and other states’ races could make the overall outcome of the midterms “a little less clear.”

The outcome with Ohio’s four House races could also “tell us much about the majority situation,” Skelley added. The race for Ohio’s 7th District, where Rep. Max Miller (R) has faced allegations of domestic abuse toward his ex-wife and daughter, is a 50-50 split in a state President Trump won in 2024.

“A Democratic win would push the party’s majority chances north of 90 percent, while a GOP hold would lower them below 65 percent,” Skelley said.

Several states will have their polls completely close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. These are: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Tennessee, in addition to Washington, D.C.

Polls across Arkansas will close at 8:30 p.m.

Most polling closes at 8 p.m. in Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas, with each state being split between time zones. The rest of the polls in these states will close at 9 p.m. The 8 p.m. hour is expected to be the busiest hour of the night.

The results from the battleground Senate races between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, Sen. Susan Collins (R) and Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine, and Ken Paxton (R) and James Talarico (D) in Texas will begin to trickle in and will provide insights into which party has the momentum.

A Rogers victory in Michigan would mark a “massive win” for the GOP, Skelley noted, as the party seeks to defend its majority. But clear Democratic victories in any of these three states could prompt calls that the party is inching closer to reclaiming the Senate.

States that will see all polls close at 9 p.m. include Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Democrats in Iowa and Republicans in Minnesota are seeking to flip open Senate seats. Iowa is one of the key battlegrounds that could decide control of Congress, with toss-up House and Senate contests.

Nebraska, meanwhile, is also a state to keep a close eye on in the 9 p.m. hour. Independent Dan Osborn is mounting a Senate comeback bid after losing to Republican Sen. Deb Fischer by single digits in the red stronghold two years ago.

Montana, Nevada and Utah will see polls close at 10 p.m., along with most of Idaho, which will also see some of its polls close at 11 p.m. Oregon will also see polls close as early as 10 p.m. for communities in the Mountain time zone, though the rest of the state’s polls close at 11 p.m.

Another independent candidate making waves is Montana’s Seth Bodnar. He faces an uphill battle against Republican Kurt Alme, who DDHQ estimates has a 77 percent chance of winning Sen. Steve Daines’s (R) open seat, as of Monday.

With the bulk of polls closed by 10 p.m., the balance of power on Capitol Hill is likely to begin to come into focus.

Two West Coast states — California and Washington — will see polls close at 11 p.m.

Western states, with some almost entirely conducting elections by mail, allow longer windows of time for ballots to arrive for counting after Election Day, notably California.

The Golden State’s votes for House candidates have proven decisive in who controls the lower chamber, including in 2022 and 2024, years in which the party in control held a narrow majority.

But its redrawn congressional map ushered in with the passage of Proposition 50 last year gives Democrats a chance of winning at least five seats, effectively shrinking the odds for competition and potentially leaving out any chances for close races that could be determined in the days that follow.

Both states could see at least one district flip. California’s 22nd District battle between incumbent Rep. David Valadao (R) and Randy Villegas (D) could shift blue, while Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) faces a tight race against state Senate Minority Leader John Braun (R) in the battleground 3rd District.

The last two states to join the union, Hawaii and Alaska, will see polls close at 12 a.m., with some of Alaska’s polls closing at 1 a.m.

Alaska’s size could leave its polls results open-ended in the hours after Election Day ends, with ballots from rural areas sometimes taking days to be counted as they are transported.

Early vote ballots in regional elections offices through the Thursday before Election Day are counted the night of the election, while ballots cast on Friday through Election Day are counted seven days after the election, according to Alaska’s Division of Elections .

Skelley told The Hill that there could be no projections for Alaska by the end of the night. A full count of who holds control of the Senate will be later than the House and “it’s just a question of how much later.”

It was around this time frame, specifically at 12:06 a.m., that The Associated Press called the Senate for Republicans in 2024. The previous two elections saw the outlet call the Senate several days later, including four days in 2022 and 64 days in 2020 because of the Georgia Senate runoff election held in December, which determined Democratic control in the upper chamber along with the incoming Biden administration.

The last midterm election cycle when the AP called the House for Democrats was at 3 a.m. the following Wednesday in 2018. However, every election since then has seen the House called for the winning party days after Election Day, according to the AP. It took one week for the House to be called in 2020 and eight days each for the 2022 and 2024 elections.
