articles.title: The House races to watch for early signs of a midterm wave
articles.summary: The House battlefield in Tuesday’s midterms comprises dozens of races in largely purple districts where majorities are won and lost. But as GOP leaders scram...
articles.body:
The House battlefield in Tuesday's midterms comprises dozens of races in largely purple districts where majorities are won and lost.

But as GOP leaders scramble against the odds to salvage their fragile majority — and the favored Democrats fight to run up the score — both sides are paying particular attention to a much smaller number of contests that might lend early hints about where the winds are blowing and whether a wave is forming.

Many of those races are on the East Coast, where the polls close first and the results are expected to arrive most quickly. But other districts have unique demographic characteristics that can reveal broader trends about which voters are animated, which are staying home, and how those dynamics might affect the overall results.

Here are the races that outside experts and campaign operatives in both parties will be watching most closely as a gauge of where the momentum is flowing on election night.

There are three races in Virginia that are competitive, to varying degrees, and experts are monitoring all three of them closely for telltale signs of broader trends.

In the 2nd District around Virginia Beach, GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans is facing a tough challenge from former Rep. Elaine Luria (D), who held the seat for two terms before Kiggans picked her off in 2022. Both candidates are Navy veterans, and both are well known among voters. Republicans see the race as an early gauge of how their battleground incumbents will fare.

"That is the bellwether district in my view," said a Republican campaign operative. "You have a well-funded incumbent going against a former member, who also has high name ID and [is] very well funded. So that will be a true test, early in the night, on how our incumbents are holding up."

Virginia's 1st District is also under a microscope. The seat is held by GOP Rep. Rob Wittman, a 20-year House veteran who was initially expected to skate to victory in a district President Trump won by 5 points in 2024. But the contest has tightened considerably in the final stretch, and the analysts at Sabato's Crystal Ball, an independent election handicapper based at the University of Virginia, say the race now leans in favor of the Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor, the top prosecutor for Henrico County.

In an even greater sign of the GOP's struggles this cycle, Republican Rep. John McGuire, a close ally of the president, is also facing stiff headwinds in the 5th District, which Trump won by 12 points just two years ago. The analysts at the Cook Political Report rate the race a toss-up. And on Monday, Sabato shifted the race in favor of the Democratic challenger, former Rep. Tom Perriello, who held the seat from 2009 to 2011.

If Perriello wins, "then the floor has fallen out from underneath Republicans," said a Democratic campaign strategist.

Kyle Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato's Crystal Ball, agreed. He said if Democrats defeat Kiggans, it would suggest they'll win control of the House; if they beat Wittman, it would signal an even greater shift in power around the country; and if McGuire falls, it would suggest a "Dem megawave."

The district comprising Lansing has been a bellwether battleground for years. The seat was held by Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a centrist Democrat, before she jumped to the Senate last year and was replaced by moderate Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, an Army veteran.

Now Democrats are hoping the current political environment will help them make Barrett a one-term lawmaker. Challenging him is William Lawrence, a liberal climate activist who, until recently , was a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

That affiliation has sparked plenty of attacks from Republicans, who say Lawrence is simply too liberal for the purple 7th District. But they also say the outcome will be a good gauge of where voters are nationally — and whether Trump is a greater liability, for Republicans, than the socialist label is for Democrats.

"William Lawrence is literally a member of the DSA. And so that's another test of: Do these further-to-the-left candidates — does that candidate-quality thing even matter?" said the GOP campaign strategist. "That's a really good seat to look at to get a sense of how the night goes."

Democrats like their chances, noting that Lawrence was one of the first candidates this cycle to tap into the widespread outrage over data centers, which has transcended region and party. He's proposing a national 12-month moratorium on building them.

"He has made data centers a central part of his pitch. I think he's also somebody who is definitely in tune with the anger that folks have on the ground in Michigan," said the Democratic strategist. "Michigan 7 is just always close, always a toss-up no matter what. And we feel good about our chances there right now."

Texas was the first GOP-led state to redraw its House map this cycle, and Republicans did it with designs to pick up five Democratic seats, largely in the south near the Mexican border. Trump made inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024, and the new lines sought to exploit that shift.

But polls indicate that Hispanic voters have soured on Trump , largely over his deportation surge, and Texas will test just how angry those voters are — and how far a potential backlash might reach.

The shift has already helped several Democratic incumbents, including Reps. Henry Cuellar in the 28th District and Vicente Gonzalez in the 34th, who appear poised to survive a redistricting process that had targeted them directly.

"I'll be honest, [in] South Texas, the bottom has fallen out," the GOP operative said. "Vicente Gonzalez looked like one of the most appetizing pickups for us, and I still do think we can get that race close. But I think with the ICE raids and the economy, especially in South Texas, it really hit us hardest."

The shift has been so pronounced that Democrats are now fighting to pick off at least one Republican incumbent, Rep. Monica De La Cruz, in the 15th District, and they're increasingly optimistic they can keep the 35th District, which was redrawn to eliminate Democratic Rep. Greg Casar. Cook rates both races as toss-ups, while Sabato puts both in the "leans Democrat" column.

"Those are the ones to keep an eye on for how much of a backlash is there to the Trump administration's overstep when it comes to ICE enforcement," said the Democratic operative, using an abbreviation for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In redrawing their House map this year at Trump's behest, Republicans in North Carolina's state House had a particular target in mind: Rep. Don Davis, a two-term Democrat who represents the northeastern corner of the state.

But the new map wasn't the knockout blow Republicans had envisioned, and in recent weeks Davis's prospects have improved for the Democrats, who are also hoping to pick up a Senate seat in the Tar Heel State. Cook rates the race a toss-up, while Sabato gives Davis a slight edge.

"He's very moderate, he's very well known around the district, and we always knew that was going to be really tough," the GOP operative acknowledged.

The contest is being viewed as an early bellwether of the Republicans' broader redistricting campaign. But in a district with a large Black population, it's also being watched closely for signs of how Black voters — who shifted toward Trump in 2024 — have responded to the president's subsequent efforts to eliminate Black districts and gut the Voting Rights Act, a seminal law of the Civil Rights Movement.

A Davis victory, the Democratic strategist said, would indicate "there's significant backlash among Black voters in the South, which could help us in other places." That includes Alabama's 2nd District, where Republicans sought to draw Rep. Shomari Figures (D) out of office.

The Keystone State is home to four battleground districts where GOP incumbents are fighting to keep their seats. How those races turn out, the experts say, will reveal much about the mood of American voters more broadly.

"If we lose all four of them, that's the majority right there. And that'll tell you how the margins are going to look," said the Republican strategist. "Pennsylvania will be the gauge of how bad it's going to be in terms of how many districts we actually lose altogether."

Three of those contests are particularly challenging for Republicans this cycle. Reps. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District, Rob Bresnahan in the 8th and Scott Perry in the 10th are all predicted to lose to their Democratic opponents, according to the analysts at Cook and Sabato.

In the 1st District, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is faring slightly better: Cook rates his race a toss-up. But Sabato analysts gave Democrats the edge in the race in the final hours before voters go to the polls.

Democrats acknowledge that Fitzpatrick, a centrist who has done more than most Republicans to distance himself from Trump, will be tough to beat. But even Republicans aren't guaranteeing victory.

For several cycles straight, Democrats have tried unsuccessfully to pick off several Republican incumbents in Iowa. How they fare this year might lend hints about the size of a blue wave, or if one arrives at all.

Republicans say they're confident that GOP Rep. Zach Nunn will win his right to a third term in the 3rd District, despite analysts predicting that Democrats will steal that seat on Tuesday. And they like their chances of keeping the 2nd District, which was vacated by GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for Senate.

But the outcome of those races will hinge on turnout for Hinson in the Senate race, which could make or break the vulnerable House GOP candidates on the ballot below her.

"If she does well on the Senate side of things, I do think Nunn's in good shape — and her open seat, as well in Iowa 2," said the Republican campaign strategist.

Republicans are less confident about another Iowa Republican, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st District, who is among the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans of the cycle.

"I wouldn't read too much into Miller-Meeks losing, because I think it's just bound to happen," said the GOP operative. "I think the better gauge is Nunn, where if he holds on, it's going to be a pretty decent night for us."

Another early-results state is Florida, where the GOP-led Legislature redrew its House map with designs to flip four Democratic seats. Kondik, the managing editor of Sabato's Crystal Ball, said the outcome of those races will predict who controls the House next year.

"See how many gerrymandered seats in Florida Dems salvage," he said. "Saving at least one is consistent with winning the House."

The redistricting effort is expected to yield at least some results for the GOP: Democratic Rep. Darren Soto is predicted to lose his seat in the 9th District after a decade on Capitol Hill. And Republicans are optimistic they will pick up the seats held by the other Democrats targeted by the new map, including Reps. Kathy Castor in the 14th District, Jared Moskowitz in the 25th and an open seat left vacant by the retiring Rep. Lois Frankel in the 22nd.

"Hispanic voters care less about the ICE raids and more about the socialism message," said the Republican strategist. "I feel really good about the Florida seats. ... I think we'll come out on top in almost all of them."

But as in the other redistricted states, polls suggest the effort is falling short of initial expectations. Moskowitz, for instance, is now favored in his race, according to both Cook and Sabato. And both handicappers rate Castor's seat and Frankel's open seat up for grabs.

articles.title: Pennsylvania takes center stage in Democrats’ push to flip the House
articles.summary: HARRISBURG, Pa. — Democrats are increasingly bullish they can deliver a major blow to Republicans in the midterms, viewing key GOP-held battleground House districts in Pennsylvania as central to their path to victory. Four of the state’s most closely-watched House races — involving Republican Reps. Scott Perry of Pennsylvania’s 10th District, Brian Fitzpatrick of the…
articles.body:
HARRISBURG, Pa. — Democrats are increasingly bullish they can deliver a major blow to Republicans in the midterms, viewing key GOP-held battleground House districts in Pennsylvania as central to their path to victory.

Four of the state’s most closely-watched House races — involving Republican Reps. Scott Perry of Pennsylvania’s 10th District, Brian Fitzpatrick of the 1st District, Rob Bresnahan of the 8th District and Ryan Mackenzie of the 7th District — have been rated as either toss-ups or lean Democrat by nonpartisan election handicappers, putting Pennsylvania squarely at the center of the battle for control of the lower chamber.

“The path to the majority runs right here through Pennsylvania,” Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.), chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said during a canvass launch Sunday in Bethlehem for Democratic House candidate Bob Brooks, who is challenging Mackenzie.

Still, Democratic challengers in Pennsylvania say they are keeping their expectations in check in the final few hours of the campaign season, haunted by a bruising 2024 election cycle and the risk of reading too much into the polls.

The stakes are enormous for both parties.

Democrats need a net gain of three seats to win back the House, while Republicans are working overtime to preserve their razor-thin margin and stave off a Democratic victory that would put President Trump and his inner circle at the center of congressional investigations and oversight.

“We will flip the House,” DelBene told The Hill. “I’m confident … but I’m also paranoid. I’m very aware that, you know, Republicans have played games — redistricting, attacking campaign finance, you know, attacking vote by mail, all these things.”

Brooks, a retired firefighter, told The Hill that while he feels good about his prospects, he can’t “take anything for granted.”

“We have to run hard. But I agree, and I think we’re going to win this seat,” Brooks said. “I think it’s crystal clear with the negative attack ads that I’ve been facing for months from Ryan Mackenzie. If he had real policy to stand on, we’d hear about that, not ‘Bad Bob.’”

Former television news anchor Janelle Stelson (D), who is challenging Perry for a second time after losing in 2024, said her Republican opponent has not lost “for a very long time.”

“We’ve been doing everything you could do, been making all the phone calls, you know, knocking on every door and sending me and the whole team everywhere we can. We’ve just been doing everything we can to try to get a win in a very Republican district because we want to represent everybody,” she said.

Stelson noted that voters are “deeply unhappy” and “really thirsty for change.”

Republicans have been contending with mounting political headwinds this cycle as voter frustration over the economy, the ongoing military conflict with Iran and Trump’s low approval ratings have left a stain on the party. Democrats are casting the midterms as a referendum on Trump — and the GOP candidates who have backed his agenda.

Trump held a tele-rally for Perry, Mackenzie and other Pennsylvania Republicans on Saturday, urging his supporters to head to the polls Tuesday.

He did not endorse Fitzpatrick, a GOP centrist who voted against the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year; supported war powers resolutions that would limit the president’s military actions in Iran; backed a Democratic effort to extend the now-expired Affordable Care Act subsidies for three years; and broken with his party on numerous other issues. Fitzpatrick represents a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential race, and the Republican lawmaker has portrayed himself as a member of Congress who’s willing to work across the aisle.

Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner challenging Fitzpatrick, said he’s confident he and his team have done “everything we need to do to win this race.”

“I don’t make predictions about elections. I’ve run in elections before,” Harvie said. “All you do is you leave everything you can out on the field … and the scoreboard shows up at the end of the night. It is what it is.”

Still, he argues that he’s heard from voters in the district who believe Fitzpatrick has fallen short of delivering for them.

High-profile Democrats and prominent party figures have descended on the Keystone State in the final stretch of the campaign to rally behind Democratic challengers and mobilize voters.

Rahm Emanuel, who served as the White House chief of staff under the Obama administration and as U.S. ambassador to Japan under the Biden administration, appeared at Harvie’s canvass launch Monday in Fairless Hills.

“You know, when you are done knocking doors across the street, you got 10 more doors to go,” Emanuel, who is eyeing a 2028 White House run, told supporters.

“When you have texted the last person and your thumb is aching and you think you have arthritis, 10 more texts to go. Phone calls, postcards, the whole gambit, everybody. This is our year because Tuesday at 7 p.m., we’re putting a period at the end of this president’s presidency. And Bucks County and Bob are going to be the exclamation point,” he added.

Malcolm Kenyatta, the Democratic National Committee’s vice chair, also addressed a crowd at Brooks’s event Sunday.

“Believe it or not, contrary to what it feels like, the job of government is to not just provide you with constant gastrointestinal discomfort. The job of government is to deliver and make people’s lives better … We can make that a reality guys,” he said.

Democrats fell just three seats short of reclaiming the House majority in 2024, with a margin of 7,309 votes between both parties — including just 4,062 votes in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, according to Inside Elections .

“When we talk about how important it is to be out, to knocking on the doors, to making phone calls, to reminding people how important their vote is, there’s nothing more important than doing that because these races can be very, very close, and a whole difference in terms of how our Congress works,” DelBene said.

Still, Democrats say the momentum building this election cycle is markedly different from what they experienced in 2024.

“I think definitely there is a lot of energy on the ground all across the country because people know how important this election is. They’ve seen the damage that’s been done by policies put in place by the administration and Republicans in Congress kind of going along with it, and they’re hurting, and so people are extremely motivated everywhere to stand up to use their voice,” DelBene said.

“And so all across the country in swing districts, there’s been huge turnout, huge excitement, because people realize how important their vote is,” she added.

Emanuel echoed similar sentiments, noting that people are “angry” at Trump and Republicans and arguing that it’s a “different motivating purpose.”

“The Republicans will lose on Tuesday. Democrats will need to win in 2027. Delivering a lobbying and ethics reform bill that actually makes changes to the culture of Washington, the corruption. Delivering a raise in the minimum wage that hasn’t been raised in 20 years. Delivering relief from these tariffs that are raising prices that families are paying. If we do that, deliver both change and the trust that people think is broken, then we’ll have won and that’s the most important,” he said.

articles.title: Your hour-by-hour guide to 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: Election Day is here, and observers waiting with bated breath for results can expect a late night. Results will begin to trickle in at 6 p.m. EST, with contr...
articles.body:
Election Day is here, and observers waiting with bated breath for results can expect a late night.

Results will begin to trickle in at 6 p.m. EST, with control of Congress on the line. Although the final tabulation of votes could take days or even weeks, race projections Tuesday night will begin to paint a picture of which party will clinch power on Capitol Hill.

Democrats need to win four GOP-held Senate seats and net three Republican House seats to flip either chamber. A later night would bode well for Republicans, particularly if key races are too close to call.

"If the polls are right, the generic ballot is relatively right, we're going to be able to project pretty early in the night," Decision Desk HQ's (DDHQ) chief election analyst Geoffrey Skelley told The Hill.

Here's what to expect every hour as the polls close Tuesday:

Kentucky and Indiana will be the first states to have some of their polls close at 6 p.m., with their remaining polls closing at 7 p.m.

Skelley wrote in an October blog post that within the first two or so hours, results reported from the eastern part of the U.S. "will drive our initial understanding of what's happening in the midterms."

A flip in Kentucky's 6th District could be indicative of a "big blue wave," Skelley said. DDHQ rates the race between Republican Ralph Alvarado and Democrat Zach Dembo for outgoing Rep. Andy Barr's (R) seat as a toss-up.

Polls close at 7 p.m. in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia and most of Florida and New Hampshire, though remaining polls in those last two states close at 8 p.m. West Virginia, Ohio and North Carolina's polls close at 7:30 p.m.

Skelley noted that the elections in eight of these states — Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Virginia — will be "especially revealing" once polls close. Nearly 50 House races in these states are "at least mildly competitive — that is, not 'safe' for one party."

The state with the quickest reporting in the country is Florida, with early data points expected to be available after closing. The Panhandle closes at 8 p.m.

Poll closings by 7:30 p.m. could show signs that a "blue wave" is coming, particularly if Democrats claim victories in Florida, Indiana, Georgia, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina and Virginia.

"An actual Democratic win in any of these seats would be an electoral earthquake that all but guarantees a Democratic majority," Skelley estimated. "Republican holds, meanwhile, would only mildly improve the GOP's majority chances."

Skelley told The Hill that after the fallout from Florida's election results in 2000, its voting system became "the best in the country" and could map out what shakes out between 7:20 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.

"We'll be able to make projections because we'll be like, 'Well, there's no way someone's ever coming that lead, or what have you,'" he said. "A lot of key districts, and a lot of Republican leading districts on paper, because of the Florida redraw –– Democrats are winning in those places. That will be like, well, it's going to be real hard for Republicans to win if they're losing in Florida like this."

He emphasized that Florida is a "mixed bag" for both parties, so results between this and other states' races could make the overall outcome of the midterms "a little less clear."

The outcome with Ohio's four House races could also "tell us much about the majority situation," Skelley added. The race for Ohio's 7th District, where Rep. Max Miller (R) has faced allegations of domestic abuse toward his ex-wife and daughter, is a 50-50 split in a state President Trump won in 2024.

"A Democratic win would push the party's majority chances north of 90 percent, while a GOP hold would lower them below 65 percent," Skelley said.

Several states will have their polls completely close at 8 p.m. Tuesday. These are: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Tennessee, in addition to Washington, D.C.

Polls across Arkansas will close at 8:30 p.m.

Most polling closes at 8 p.m. in Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas, with each state being split between time zones. The rest of the polls in these states will close at 9 p.m. The 8 p.m. hour is expected to be the busiest hour of the night.

The results from the battleground Senate races between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, Sen. Susan Collins (R) and Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine, and Ken Paxton (R) and James Talarico (D) in Texas will begin to trickle in and will provide insights into which party has the momentum.

A Rogers victory in Michigan would mark a "massive win" for the GOP, Skelley noted, as the party seeks to defend its majority. But clear Democratic victories in any of these three states could prompt calls that the party is inching closer to reclaiming the Senate.

States that will see all polls close at 9 p.m. include Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

Democrats in Iowa and Republicans in Minnesota are seeking to flip open Senate seats. Iowa is one of the key battlegrounds that could decide control of Congress, with toss-up House and Senate contests.

Nebraska, meanwhile, is also a state to keep a close eye on in the 9 p.m. hour. Independent Dan Osborn is mounting a Senate comeback bid after losing to Republican Sen. Deb Fischer by single digits in the red stronghold two years ago.

Montana, Nevada and Utah will see polls close at 10 p.m., along with most of Idaho, which will also see some of its polls close at 11 p.m. Oregon will also see polls close as early as 10 p.m. for communities in the Mountain time zone, though the rest of the state's polls close at 11 p.m.

Another independent candidate making waves is Montana's Seth Bodnar. He faces an uphill battle against Republican Kurt Alme, who DDHQ estimates has a 77 percent chance of winning Sen. Steve Daines's (R) open seat, as of Monday.

With the bulk of polls closed by 10 p.m., the balance of power on Capitol Hill is likely to begin to come into focus.

Two West Coast states — California and Washington — will see polls close at 11 p.m.

Western states, with some almost entirely conducting elections by mail, allow longer windows of time for ballots to arrive for counting after Election Day, notably California.

The Golden State's votes for House candidates have proven decisive in who controls the lower chamber, including in 2022 and 2024, years in which the party in control held a narrow majority.

But its redrawn congressional map ushered in with the passage of Proposition 50 last year gives Democrats a chance of winning at least five seats, effectively shrinking the odds for competition and potentially leaving out any chances for close races that could be determined in the days that follow.

Both states could see at least one district flip. California's 22nd District battle between incumbent Rep. David Valadao (R) and Randy Villegas (D) could shift blue, while Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) faces a tight race against state Senate Minority Leader John Braun (R) in the battleground 3rd District.

The last two states to join the union, Hawaii and Alaska, will see polls close at 12 a.m., with some of Alaska's polls closing at 1 a.m.

Alaska's size could leave its polls results open-ended in the hours after Election Day ends, with ballots from rural areas sometimes taking days to be counted as they are transported.

Early vote ballots in regional elections offices through the Thursday before Election Day are counted the night of the election, while ballots cast on Friday through Election Day are counted seven days after the election, according to Alaska's Division of Elections .

Skelley told The Hill that there could be no projections for Alaska by the end of the night. A full count of who holds control of the Senate will be later than the House and "it's just a question of how much later."

It was around this time frame, specifically at 12:06 a.m., that The Associated Press called the Senate for Republicans in 2024. The previous two elections saw the outlet call the Senate several days later, including four days in 2022 and 64 days in 2020 because of the Georgia Senate runoff election held in December, which determined Democratic control in the upper chamber along with the incoming Biden administration.

The last midterm election cycle when the AP called the House for Democrats was at 3 a.m. the following Wednesday in 2018. However, every election since then has seen the House called for the winning party days after Election Day, according to the AP. It took one week for the House to be called in 2020 and eight days each for the 2022 and 2024 elections.

articles.title: Supreme Court hears Catholic plea to participate in Colorado preschool program
articles.summary: The Supreme Court hears arguments over whether Catholic entities should be exempted from Colorado’s anti-discrimination rules for its taxpayer-funded preschool program.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Tackling the latest in a series of cases that pit LGBTQ and religious rights against each other, the Supreme Court on Tuesday will consider whether Catholic entities should be exempted from the state’s antidiscrimination rules so they can participate in a taxpayer-funded preschool program. In the Election Day session, the justices will weigh whether Colorado’s refusal to grant an accommodation violates the religious rights of the Archdiocese of Denver and other plaintiffs under the Constitution’s First Amendment. It is the latest in a series of cases in which Christian plaintiffs have pushed back against antidiscrimination measures aimed at protecting LGBTQ rights. Most such cases considered by the Supreme Court in the past decade have arisen from Colorado. The court has a 6-3 conservative majority that regularly favors religious rights in cases brought by Christian groups. At issue is a provision of state law that bars preschools from participating in the state-funded program if they refuse admission to children based on the sexual orientation or gender identity of the child or parents. As Catholic doctrine does not recognize same-sex relationships or transgender status, the plaintiffs say the rule conflicts with their religious rights. The case is “uncomplicated,” the archdiocese’s lawyers at religious liberty group Becket said in court papers, because Colorado “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise.” The Catholic plaintiffs have the backing of the Trump administration. The preschool program, approved as part of a statewide referendum in 2020, provides taxpayer funds for parents to send their children to their preferred preschool. The state’s lawyers, led by Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat, said in their own court filing that religious schools can and do participate in the program as long as they agree to abide by the antidiscrimination provision. The Catholic preschools “want to receive public funding without complying with those conditions,” they added. The case before the justices on Tuesday focuses on the long-running question of whether excluding religious groups from certain government programs violates the Constitution’s First Amendment, which protects the free exercise of religion. In a 1990 ruling called Employment Division v. Smith, the Supreme Court stated that religious exemptions are not required when a law applies equally to everyone. The court has stopped short of overturning that ruling in recent cases, even as it has ruled in favor of religious plaintiffs. In a notable ruling in 2021, the court ruled that a Catholic group could not be barred from a Philadelphia foster care program because of its views opposing same-sex couples. The Catholic challengers in the Colorado case argue, among other things, that the state program already contains some loopholes that allow for schools to apply some discretion when accepting children. They are allowed, for example, to prioritize children with disabilities and those from low-income families. Those allowances “expressly conflict” with the state’s equal access requirement, the challengers wrote in court papers. In a separate line of recent rulings, the Supreme Court has also paved the way for taxpayer money to flow to religious groups, including schools, despite longstanding prohibitions driven by the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause, which bars government endorsement of religion. Colorado argues that its allowance for specialized services for disabled children and low-income families is consistent with its equal access approach because it “advances Colorado’s interests” in ensuring that disadvantaged people are not denied entry to the preschools, the state’s lawyers wrote. Separately, preschools operated by Catholic Charities do participate in the state program. That organization has a different mission from the preschools run directly by the church and does not require attendees to comply with Catholic teachings. The other plaintiffs in Tuesday’s case are St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton and Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood, plus two parishioners at St. Mary, Daniel and Lisa Sheley. The Sheleys have seven children, with one in preschool and another soon to follow. The Sheleys have not been able to benefit from more than $12,000 in tuition assistance because they chose to send their children to the church’s preschool, their lawyers said. The archdiocese operates 34 preschools in the state in total. The challengers sued in 2023 but lost in lower courts before asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

images.caption: The Supreme Court is hearing arguments on Catholic preschools that are challenging their exclusion from Colorado's universal preschool program. Preschools in the program have to agree to nondiscrimination, including on sexual orientation and gender ID, which these Catholic preschools won't do.

articles.title: DOJ faces ‘heavy lift’ in Alaska election appeal as separate criminal probe continues
articles.summary: DOJ faces an uphill battle appealing the dismissed Alaska Senate ballot lawsuit over two Dan Sullivan candidates before Election Day polls close.
articles.body: The Justice Department faces an uphill legal battle in its bid to overturn a federal judge's dismissal of its Alaska Senate election lawsuit, according to legal experts who questioned whether the government can secure meaningful relief before voting ends Tuesday — even as a separate criminal investigation continues. DOJ filed a notice of appeal after Obama-appointed U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed its lawsuit Sunday over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot. The judge ruled that federal officials lacked standing because they had not demonstrated how their proposed remedy could address potential voter confusion without compromising ballot secrecy. With voting ending Tuesday, attorneys told Fox News Digital that even a successful appeal could leave the government scrambling to obtain an injunction or return to district court, while a defeat would leave the civil case dismissed without necessarily affecting potential criminal charges arising from the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan. DOJ SET TO APPEAL RULING IN ALASKA SENATE RACE DISPUTE OVER ‘DECOY DAN’ "The federal judge dismissed on a procedural issue — standing," election attorney Jason Torchinsky of Virginia-based firm Holtzman Vogel told Fox News Digital. "So if the government were to prevail, it would either have to seek injunctive relief from the appeals court in the first instance, a very high bar, or go back down to the district court to seek relief." "Given the time available between now and close of polls [Tuesday], this is a heavy lift for the government," Torchinsky added. A reversal would not automatically change Alaska's election results. DOJ would still need to obtain specific judicial relief, potentially requiring further proceedings in district court. Former federal prosecutor and ex-Pentagon official Cully Stimson similarly said that DOJ will have difficulty securing any immediate relief in its effort to pause the Sullivan-Peltola contest. While Gleason was appointed by Obama, Stimson suggested the ruling did not appear partisan and said uncertainty remains because voting had not yet concluded. "I'm not surprised that the judge did this. I don't think it would matter whether an Obama judge or any other judge appointed by any other president," Stimson told Fox News Digital. "Asking for injunctive relief way before anything even happens is a reach," he said, adding Alaska falls under the San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit, which will hear any appeal. But Stimson suggested DOJ may have a longer-term objective beyond winning an immediate injunction: establishing a legal record that could support further proceedings after the election, once the votes are counted. TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS "They may be filing these suits to establish a record and force Alaska and others supporting the status quo to defend what's happening, knowing that there's some level of confusion, and they have the legal wheels churning," he said. "So after the vote is [over], they've started the legal wheels rolling." Former Assistant U.S. Attorney for North Florida Zack Smith added that if the Ninth Circuit does not hear the case promptly, DOJ could seek emergency review from the U.S. Supreme Court. While the Alaska case is considered unprecedented, according to the experts, the idea of a Supreme Court expedition at election time is not. On Dec. 9, 2000, one day after the Florida Supreme Court ordered a manual recount of disputed ballots in the Bush v. Gore presidential election dispute involving "hanging chads," then-Texas Gov. George W. Bush’s legal team successfully sought emergency intervention. The court ultimately decided in Bush’s favor within a week. Since the disputed 2000 election, which featured "hanging chads" on hole-punched paper ballots and the Brooks Brothers Riot at the Miami-Dade elections office, DOJ has become well-accustomed to the expedited-review process, the experts said. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS "DOJ is familiar with kind of working quickly, getting things to the Supreme Court, and so I wouldn't be completely surprised if you were to see something like that," Smith said. Bush v. Gore offers a procedural parallel because federal courts were asked to intervene in the administration of a state-run election. "Florida was conducting the election in the manner under Florida law, under this time, place and manners set out by Florida law even though it was a federal election," Stimson said. "They used a particular type of ballot, which had those so-called dangling chads, which were punch-holes that didn't come the whole way off, so the hole was left with a little tag, essentially like a skin tag, and eventually the Supreme Court of Florida ruled." "But because there were federal violations, eventually the Supreme Court weighed in and stopped it. And at no point in time had the vice president’s (Albert Gore) vote count ever surpassed that of the governor (Bush) and because it was a federal interest, the Supreme Court stepped in and stopped this counting at the state level." Alex Charns, an attorney who has argued in federal court, told Fox News Digital that the clock has run out and DOJ's goal of segregating ballots based on voter intent is no longer possible. "I've litigated against the USDOJ for over thirteen years in federal court. I've practiced law in Durham, N.C., for 43 years. The USDOJ filed a case without legal merit and its appeal is likely to fail," he said. "In addition, voting ends [Tuesday]. The relief they seek isn't possible — ballots already cast can't be segregated. Also, one cannot tell why any voter voted in a particular way. The appeal is unlikely to be successful." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In a statement from the DOJ's "Rapid Response" (DOJ-RR) office, a spokesperson said the court "dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters." "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," DOJ-RR said, announcing their appeal. Stimson cautioned that the outcome of the civil litigation would have little bearing on the separate criminal investigation, which could uncover evidence supporting additional legal action even if DOJ's appeal fails. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As long as that criminal investigation is going on, you're not breathing easy," he said, adding that evidence uncovered by federal investigators could potentially provide grounds for a separate civil lawsuit.

articles.title: First polls open as voters to decide control of Congress
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - Polls are open in several eastern states as the final hours of the 2026 midterm elections begin and control of Congress hangs in the ba...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) - Polls are open in several eastern states as the final hours of the 2026 midterm elections begin and control of Congress hangs in the balance.

Several key states across the country are open for voting and will continue to accept voters until late in the night. The Center Square plans coverage of more than 80 races across the country on Tuesday night.

Here is a guide for when polls open and close across the country.

6 a.m. ET - CT, IN, Maine, KY, NY, NJ, VA, VT

Polls in Connecticut, Indiana, Maine, Kentucky, New York, New Jersey, Virginia and Vermont will be the first in the country to see voters at the polls on Election Day. Each state is in the Eastern time zone and accepts voters beginning at 6 a.m.

A critical race for control of the U.S. Senate takes place in Maine between Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic candidate Troy Jackson.

Jackson leads 49% to 46.4% in the average of five most recent polls compiled by 270toWin.

Kentucky and Indiana both close polling locations at 6 p.m. Eastern and could offer insight on partisan fortunes throughout the remainder of the night.

Polls in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia open beginning at 6:30 a.m. Eastern. Both Ohio and North Carolina have critical federal races on the ballot that will determine control of Congress.

The race between U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, and Democrat Sherrod Brown has faced intense speculation over a winner. The Cook Political Report ranks the race as a "toss up," meaning either candidate has a chance of winning the seat for Vice President JD Vance's remaining term, which ends in 2029.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, faces Republican Michael Whatley in the state's competitive Senate race as well.

Polls close at 7:30 p.m. Eastern in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.

7 a.m. ET/ 6 a.m. CT - FL, GA, DE, IL, IA, MI, RI, SC, PA, MO, MA, MD, LA

Polls open in most remaining states across the East Coast beginning at 7 a.m. on Election Day. Florida, Georgia, Delaware, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and Maryland will all see voters head to the polls in critical races down the ballot.

Missouri, Louisiana and Illinois will also see voters begin hitting the polls, although their local time will read 6 a.m. Polls close in Missouri and Illinois at 7 p.m. Central and in Louisiana at 8 p.m. Central.

8 a.m. ET/7 a.m. CT - AL, IA, KS, MN, MS, ND, OK, SD, TX, WI

More states across the Central time zone will begin opening polls at 8 a.m. Eastern, when it is 7 a.m. local. Across the House and Senate, Iowa and Texas will see voters head to the polls in crucial races that are predicted to be extremely tight.

Texas voters will also be affected by redistricting in as many as five congressional districts that sought to lean in favor of Republicans during the midterm elections. Polls will close in most of these states by 9 p.m. Eastern.

Arkansas is the only state in the country where polls will open at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Voters in the state will decide on a U.S. Senate race expected to favor Republican incumbent Tom Cotton, significant U.S. House races and other measures down the ballot.

9 a.m. ET/7 a.m. MT - AZ, CO, MT, NE, NM, Utah, WY

As the morning goes on, polling locations in states across the Mountain time zone will begin to see voters. Nebraska, divided between the Central and Mountain time zones, will see polls open at 7 a.m. MT in both regions.

Crucial races for control of the U.S. House of Representatives will occur throughout these states and down ballot measures will have a significant impact on the makeup of state legislatures.

10 a.m. ET/ 7a.m. PT - CA, ID, NV, OR, WA

States along the West Coast and across the Pacific time zone will see polls open beginning at 7 a.m. A test of California's redistricting in favor of Democrats will likely be top of mind for voters heading to the polls.

Poll openings in Washington and Oregon are subject to county-level discretion. Both states rely on mail-in voting to conduct elections. Polls will close in these states at 11 p.m. Eastern.

Alaska will see polls open at 7 a.m. Alaska Standard Time or 11 a.m. Eastern Standard Time. The crucial U.S. Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola will be key in control of the upper chamber in Congress.

Polls will not close in Alaska until 8 p.m. local time, or 1 a.m. Eastern time.

Additionally, while no specific time is listed, polls in New Hampshire must also be open by 11 a.m. ET on Election Day.

Hawaii will be the final state in the country to see polls open at 7 a.m. Hawaii Standard Time and Noon Eastern Time. Federal and statewide elections throughout the island will also contribute to control of Congress.

To stay updated on election results, visit thecentersquare.com/elections .

articles.title: Polls open in closely contested US midterm elections 2026
articles.summary: Democrats are eyeing historic gains in the US Congress that could change the trajectory of the country.
articles.body:
Polls have opened in some parts of the United States for Tuesday’s pivotal midterm elections, with all 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats being contested .

Voting hours are determined and set by each state. Polls have already opened in a majority of states, with a handful of remaining states set to start election day voting soon.

More than 57 million Americans have already cast early ballots, with some of the heaviest voting coming from some of this year’s biggest political battlegrounds: Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.

Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.

Republicans currently have a majority (53) in the 100-seat Senate. Democrats and independents who caucus with the party hold 47. Republicans also have a narrow four-seat majority in the House.

Democrats have campaigned on promises to address the nation’s cost-of-living crisis and end Trump’s war on Iran.

They are eyeing historic gains in both houses of Congress that could ultimately change the trajectory of the US president’s final two years in office.

Republicans, however, are hoping to defy political gravity.

Despite Trump’s near record-low approval ratings and a historical precedent for significant midterm losses by the sitting US president’s party, conservative and right-leaning candidates are banking on their most loyal voters and distrust of progressive politics to help turn the tide on Democrats’ expected gains.

Tuesday’s midterms also come on the back of Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over her party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, on Sunday.

Shortly after polls opened this morning, a malfunction in voting machines was reported in New York’s Westchester County amid a countywide issue with machines that aren’t accepting paper ballots.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said her office “is monitoring the scanner issue in Westchester and is in contact with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a resolution”. “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count,” James said in a post on X.

articles.title: Federal judge orders DOJ to ensure poll monitors are not law enforcement officials
articles.summary: The NAACP failed to block Justice Department poll monitors, but a federal judge barred armed officers and anyone with arrest power on Election Day.
articles.body: A federal judge denied the NAACP’s request to block the Justice Department from sending election monitors to polling places, but ordered the department to ensure they are not sworn law enforcement officers and cannot make arrests. U.S. District Judge Reggie Walton, in an order Monday night, said the DOJ must also ensure its monitors are unarmed, out of uniform and do not display insignia identifying them as federal employees. The order applies to the department’s poll monitoring program for Election Day, Nov. 3. BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS VOTER-FRAUD PROBES IN BATTLEGROUND STATES JUST DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS "The Court is therefore unpersuaded by the plaintiffs' assertion that a person who is simply ‘project[ing a] command[ing] presence, scan[ning] crowds, and more’ – without any outward indications of law enforcement authority – would generate objectively reasonable fear in a voter," according to Walton, who was nominated to the Washington, D.C., court by former President George W. Bush. "Thus, the Court finds that in conjunction with the defendants’ public statements regarding voter fraud and election integrity, the deployment of these individuals as election monitors would not place the average voter 'in reasonable fear of harassment and interference with their right to vote.'" The NAACP had sought a temporary restraining order barring the DOJ from deploying personnel from agencies including the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Prisons. The group argued their presence could intimidate voters and violate the Voting Rights Act. Walton denied the motion without prejudice, finding that the current record did not show the NAACP was likely to succeed on its claim. He said the DOJ’s representations at a hearing addressed his concerns: the monitors would be administrative or clerical employees, not sworn officers, and would not carry firearms. TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE SLAMS DOOR ON DOJ AS COURT LOSSES PILE UP DAYS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS "The Court will order that the defendants comply with their counsel’s concession that they will take action to ensure that the monitors participating in the DOJ’s Poll Monitoring Program are indeed administrative or clerical personnel and not law enforcement officials, will not be in uniform or display any other insignia indicating their affiliation with a federal agency, will not be armed with a firearm, and will not have the power to effectuate arrests," Walton wrote. Walton also ordered monitors not to interfere with voters or election officials, to follow state and local rules, and to avoid speaking with voters inside polling places. They may speak with voters outside only after they have cast a ballot. Monitors must introduce themselves to election officials and carry federal credentials in case they are asked to verify their employment. Walton ordered the DOJ to file a status report by 7 a.m. ET on Tuesday explaining how it confirmed that none of the monitors would be law enforcement officials with arrest powers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The ruling followed allegations that the DOJ planned to send more than 1,000 personnel, including law enforcement agents and investigators, to polling locations. The department’s attorneys told the court that sworn agents and officers would be excluded from the program. Fox News’ Jake Gibson contributed to this report.

articles.title: Federal judge tosses Trump admin Harvard admissions lawsuit, leaves door open to future challenge
articles.summary: A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against Harvard University over admissions records, citing procedural deficiencies.
articles.body: A federal judge on Monday dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to force Harvard University to turn over admissions records as part of an investigation into whether the Ivy League school continues to consider race in its admissions process. U.S. District Judge Myong Joun ruled that the Justice Department had not adequately established that it followed required procedures before suing Harvard to obtain applicant-level admissions data. The dismissal was issued without prejudice, leaving the door open for the administration to file another lawsuit if it addresses the procedural deficiencies identified by the court. "The Government may be able to identify a qualifying determination or cure the procedural deficiency, but it has not supplied a sufficient basis for the judicial relief currently sought," Joun wrote in his 10-page decision. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACCUSES PRESTIGIOUS LAW SCHOOL OF FAVORING BLACK APPLICANTS OVER WHITE, ASIAN PEERS The Justice Department filed its lawsuit in February, alleging that Harvard had failed to cooperate with a federal civil rights review examining whether the university's admissions practices comply with the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling limiting the use of race in college admissions. The Justice Department alleged that Harvard repeatedly delayed producing requested documents and failed to provide individualized admissions records despite multiple requests and extended deadlines. JUDGE’S HARVARD ANTISEMITISM RULING SENDS TRUMP JUSTICE DEPARTMENT BACK TO DRAWING BOARD In announcing the lawsuit in February, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi accused Harvard of withholding information necessary for the government's review. "Harvard has failed to disclose the data we need to ensure that its admissions are free of discrimination," Bondi said at the time. Joun acknowledged that federal officials had made repeated requests for records and warned Harvard of potential enforcement action. But the judge found that the government's court filings failed to adequately demonstrate that officials had followed the required procedures before seeking judicial intervention. In particular, Joun noted that the Justice Department's complaint did not allege that officials had notified Harvard of their intent to pursue litigation if the university failed to comply or adequately identified the specific compliance failure at issue. HARVARD, NYU AMONG 30 UNIVERSITIES HIT WITH PENTAGON FOREIGN-TIE AUDIT DEADLINE Joun also found that the Department of Education had not sufficiently demonstrated that it followed its own required procedures before referring its separate admissions investigation for judicial enforcement. Harvard's attorneys argued that the lawsuit was part of a broader retaliatory campaign by the Trump administration after the university resisted demands for changes to its governance and academic policies, according to Reuters. The judge did not rule on Harvard's retaliation claims, stressing that his decision addressed procedural deficiencies rather than whether the university had violated federal civil rights law. "Nothing in this decision converts the Government's request for information into an accusation of present discrimination or resolves Harvard's underlying Title VI compliance," the judge wrote. articles.title: In top Senate race states, gas and grocery costs rose faster than the national average
articles.summary: From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation say the economy is their top issue this Election Day.
articles.body:
From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.

In 2024, President Donald Trump's promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.

But nearly two years into his second term, Trump's tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters .

These frustrations aren't confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll.

This has created an opening for Democrats to win majorities in both the House and the Senate. And while the House majority is widely expected to shift to Democrats after Tuesday night, the Senate is still very much a jump ball.

Veteran election data analysts are quick to remind the public that as Tuesday's voting and later counting unfolds, any one of the competitive Senate races could tip either way.

In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period.

Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof.

Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News' gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16.

In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%.

All three states broke for Trump in 2024. But two years later, they are in play, and Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, will be very closely watched Tuesday night.

Drivers in Michigan are also experiencing an outsized jump, with gas up 51% from $2.99 in February to $4.52 Monday. There, Democrat Abdul El Sayed is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers.

In Ohio, where Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging incumbent Republican Jon Husted, the price of a gallon of gas has climbed by 48%.

"We aren't going very many places," Kathy DiCristofaro, of Youngstown, Ohio, told NBC News. "We're retired and have had to cancel trips," she said.

In Maine, the price of a gallon of gas is 46% higher than it was before the war, creating a drag on Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and an opportunity for Democrat Troy Jackson.

Even when national average gas prices pivot lower, as they did throughout October, that doesn't always extend to parts of the country where refinery activity influences fuel costs, particularly in the Great Lakes region.

Far from the coasts, refineries that service Michigan, Ohio and Iowa cannot easily restore supply lost to weather events or refinery capacity.

"When you're isolated in the interior of the country, these problems can linger as long as the refinery is experiencing issues," said Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst at GasBuddy.

Beyond the gas pump, voters are also feeling the sting of higher oil prices overseas in the form of increased transportation costs for groceries and retail goods.

In several of the states with tight Senate races, average households are spending a lot more of their monthly income on groceries than shoppers elsewhere in the country, according to a WalletHub study.

Among the 10 most cost-burdened cities for groceries in America, three of them are in Ohio: Cleveland, Toledo and Cincinnati.

Also making the list are Detroit, and Hialeah, Florida, the latter a red state with surprisingly competitive gubernatorial and Senate races this year.

"The cost of living is extremely high," said Peris Morgan, a Michigan voter who spoke with NBC News outside a polling place in Sterling Heights on Monday. "Rent is high. Groceries are high, gas is high, everything is high, and so yeah, the cost of living compared to what people are being paid is not adding up."

While higher diesel costs have raised the price of transporting everyday goods, many businesses have also passed another big new cost on to consumers in the past two years: tariffs.

Trump's sweeping tariff regime has hit several of the states with major Senate races significantly harder than it has hit other states.

Three of the four states that pay the most for tariffs also have tight Senate races: Texas comes in second, Michigan third and Georgia is fourth. Further down the list, Florida, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina are all among the top 15.

The lion's share of these costs have come in the form of new import duties that affected the price of cars and trucks.

But across the country, tariffs will cost every household an additional $1,100 this year, on average, according to estimates from the Yale Budget Lab.

"This is not what we signed on for, for the tariffs and all this stuff," said Jacqui Rose Tucker, a resident of Southwest Atlanta who spoke with NBC News' Gabriella Rudy outside a grocery store.

"My dollar does not go very far anymore," she said, "This little bit of groceries was $218. It's ridiculous. So yeah, I'm real concerned."

While daily costs are straining people's wallets, longer-term investments like housing are also forcing voters to make sacrifices.

In Alaska, the median home price in September was up by 4.0% year over year at $415,805, above the national average of $389,601 which was down 0.1%, according to data from Redfin .

In Ohio , while median home prices are still below the national average, prospective buyers in September saw prices rise by 5.6% year over year across the state.

States with tight Senate races are also overrepresented on Redfin's list of cities where the price of a home has risen the most over the past year:

In Akron, Ohio, average home prices are up 22% from last year, while in Cleveland they've risen by 13%.

Joining Akron and Cleveland are Miami, metro Atlanta, Charleston, South Carolina and Cedar Rapids, Iowa — all in the top 10.

As housing prices increase in many desirable metro areas, however, higher borrowing costs at the same time are putting homeownership out of reach for many younger voters, especially Gen Z and millennials.

The average interest rate on a 30-year-fixed mortgage Monday was 7.27%.

While Americans are technically earning more in dollar terms on average, paychecks are not keeping up with the pace of inflation.

Wages in September grew by 3.0% year over year. But the annual inflation rate hit 3.7%. Adjusting for inflation, this means average hourly earnings nationwide fell by about 0.7%.

This disparity is another source of economic pressure on voters going into Election Day.

But the gap between wage growth and inflation is significantly wider in some of the states that will be most closely watched Tuesday night.

In Nebraska, purchasing power fell by 3.5% over the three months ending in August, relative to regional inflation. Iowa saw a drop of 2.6%. And in Alaska, real pay fell by 2.0% compared to the same period last year .

"I work extraordinarily hard. I'm a single mom. I've got three kids," said Jennie Larson, who planned to vote Tuesday morning in Iowa and spoke with NBC News in West Des Moines. "I go out to eat once a week, right? That's like my one luxury. But outside of that, like the gas prices, the food prices, it's unbelievable."

Tariffs have helped to drive the price of household necessities higher this year, while the rise in diesel prices has made trucking more expensive. (Joe Raedle / Getty)

articles.summary: Midterm election voters in seven Florida counties face temporary polling location changes after heavy rainfall triggered flash flood warnings.
articles.body: Florida voters in seven counties are being directed to temporary polling locations Tuesday, after widespread flooding prompted Gov. Ron DeSantis to issue an emergency order allowing election officials to relocate voting sites ahead of the midterm elections. The Florida Department of State confirmed polling-place changes in Brevard, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties, according to its website, which was updated on Election Day. DeSantis signed Executive Order 26-227 on Monday after a low-pressure system brought heavy rainfall across parts of Florida from Oct. 31 through Nov. 2, triggering flash flood warnings and threatening roads, schools and other critical infrastructure. ELECTION DAY 2026: JOIN AMERICA'S CONVERSATION HERE! The order declared a state of emergency in Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee, Highlands, Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. Fenn Center. The state cautioned that relocations remain subject to change as additional information becomes available. articles.title: Trump says Israel will stop receiving $4B in US aid by year's end, can still buy weapons
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says Benjamin Netanyahu raised the idea of ending $4 billion in U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. aid to Israel would end at the close of the year, arguing that the country no longer needs the assistance and can purchase its own weapons. "We were giving them $4 billion – we are – but it gets cut off at the end of the year," Trump told "Fox & Friends" on Tuesday in an Election Day morning announcement. Trump acknowledged the political nature of the news, pointing to Michigan's battleground Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO' "Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it?" Trump said. The support included "things and money," according to Trump, calling it military aid, cash or "barter." He said he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed ending the assistance for years, adding that Netanyahu raised the idea. "They don’t need it," Trump said. "Israel's our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it." "Israel is a very thriving country," he added. NETANYAHU DETAILS 'FINAL' CONVERSATION WITH LINDSEY GRAHAM, SAYS SENATOR CHALLENGED HIS PUSH TO END ISRAEL AID The current U.S.-Israel security assistance agreement provides about $3.8 billion annually through 2028. Netanyahu has previously said he wants to phase out Israel’s reliance on U.S. military aid, though the timing and terms of any change to the agreement have not been detailed. Trump said the assistance had become a political target, adding that Netanyahu understood "this is one of their points of contention." Trump added the $4 billion referred to military hardware or cash. "I’m going to put it in any way you want to define it," Trump said. "You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash. It’s what we give them — $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it." NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE Trump negotiated the new deal with Netanyahu, who is also facing a difficult election season with his future still up in the air as the balance of power in the Knesset tries to settle on a coalition government amid multifront wars with terrorists and Iran. "I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money," he said. "He brought it up. He said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.’" EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY Israel can still buy U.S. weapons, Trump stressed. "They can buy whatever they want," he said. Trump pointed to his administration's 2024 campaign vows to curb free foreign aid and cut government spending, just hours before the balance of congressional power will be determined for his final two years in office. SEN RAND PAUL: OUR BUDGET DEFICIT IS OUT OF CONTROL. CONGRESS MUST PASS MY SIX PENNY PLAN "We've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money," Trump said. "You know, somebody that wants to have a balanced budget. I'd love to be able to balance our budget." We have a fed that's, you know, populated by Obama and Biden people, and they don't want to do the right thing."

articles.title: Democrats’ advantage on generic ballot narrows: Survey
articles.summary: Democrats are seeing a narrow lead as voters head to the polls Tuesday, according to a new survey. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, released Monday, found that 46 per...
articles.body:
Democrats are seeing a narrow lead as voters head to the polls Tuesday, according to a new survey.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll , released Monday, found that 46 percent of registered voters said they would back Democrats in congressional races, compared with 38 percent who favored Republicans. That margin narrowed from an 11-point Democratic advantage in a similar poll conducted a week earlier.

The findings underscore the political challenges facing Republicans as they fight to maintain control of Congress. Democrats currently hold an 8.6-point lead on the generic congressional ballot, according to Decision Desk HQ polling averages.

Meanwhile, President Trump's approval rating remains underwater. The data shows just 32 percent of Americans approve of Trump's job performance. That is unchanged from last week and 1 point above the record low of 31 percent recorded in October.

Trump also appears to be a motivating factor for some independent voters , with 50 percent saying they view their congressional vote as a vote against the current administration. Just 13 percent said they were voting in support of the president, while another 33 percent said he would not influence their decision.

His low approval rating comes amid growing frustration over the cost of living , driven in part by rising fuel prices as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continues ahead of Election Day.

The national average price for a gallon of gas sits at $4.15 as of Tuesday morning, according to AAA , up more than a dollar from a year ago.

Affordability concerns and dissatisfaction with the president's agenda were top of mind for voters heading to cast their ballots.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online among 1,765 U.S. adults ahead of Election Day. It has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: 9th Circuit block on California noncitizen voter probe lifted, then restored in legal boomerang
articles.summary: A 9th Circuit panel briefly lifted a block on DOJ noncitizen voting investigations in California, but the full 11-judge court reversed course overnight.
articles.body: A federal appeals court briefly lifted a block on the Trump administration’s efforts to investigate alleged voting by noncitizens in California, then reversed course hours later, sending the dispute to the full 11-judge 9th Circuit for rehearing. Earlier Monday night, a three-judge panel granted the Justice Department’s request to pause a temporary restraining order issued by a San Francisco federal judge. That order had barred the administration from making further requests to set aside ballots under the warning of prosecution of state and local election officials who declined. The panel said the government was likely to prevail in arguing that its requests and criminal investigations were core executive functions. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS Hours later, the full 9th Circuit vacated the ruling and ordered the case reheard by all 11 active judges, according to the court’s order. The move restored the district court’s restrictions while the full court considers the dispute. "The TRO issued by a San Francisco judge purporting to restrict DOJ investigations into election officials has been appropriately lifted," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on X before the temporary restraining order was restored. "Conducting criminal investigations is a core function of the executive branch, not the judiciary." The case against the investigation of alleged noncitizen voting was brought by labor unions and civil rights groups, including the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens. They argued that DOJ and Homeland Security letters to election officials, which warned of potential criminal liability over ballots linked to suspected noncitizens, amounted to intimidation. CALIFORNIA ELECTION WORKERS HIT WITH CRIMINAL SUBPOENAS AS TRUMP DOJ TURNS UP HEAT IN VOTING SHOWDOWN The Trump administration argues that allowing illegal voting and halting investigative work could lead to prosecution for those involved. "Americans deserve to have confidence in their elections," Essayli wrote late Monday night. "The courts have made it clear that the preferred remedy for election law violations is criminal prosecution. Building on Operation Protect the Vote, we will continue investigating and charging those who violate election laws or assist in their violation." The appeals court whiplash followed a separate Supreme Court rejection of the Trump administration's effort to protect the vote Monday. The justices denied an emergency request to require California to set aside mail ballots from roughly 20,000 registered voters federal officials flagged as likely noncitizens. BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent ​McCotter wrote on X. The administration had demanded that California separate any alleged unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be U.S. citizens through investigations that the state has rejected without review. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the Justice Department wrote in its request to the Supreme Court. DHS OFFICIAL VOWS TO PROSECUTE AND DEPORT NONCITIZENS CAUGHT ILLEGALLY VOTING AHEAD OF MIDTERMS The DOJ has been forced into a legal Catch-22 where it has to watch votes be cast in California, even if they have alleged evidence of them being noncitizen voters, and then pursue legal action afterward. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that 63 people were charged with election crimes Monday. "Today's announcement marks the largest surge of voter-fraud arrests since President [Donald] Trump returned to office," Blanche wrote in a statement. "These foreign nationals allegedly took advantage of the trust of the American people and flouted the laws that govern our nation’s elections. This Department of Justice will continue investigating and prosecuting voter fraud to restore confidence in our electoral system." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The DOJ has charged 195 illegal immigrants across 25 states with illegal voting and voter registration offenses in the past nine weeks. There have been charges against 239 people with voting fraud offenses since Trump returned to the White House, according to the DOJ.

articles.title: Jose Luis Martínez-Almeida confirma que se han retirado de la Puerta del Sol 36,2 toneladas de residuos, un 88,2 % más que en el 15-M
articles.standfirst: Casi el doble de basura que la generada en la acampada de 2011
articles.summary: Casi el doble de basura que la generada en la acampada de 2011
articles.body: Este martes, 3 de noviembre, se ha producido el desalojo de la acampada que se mantenía desde hace varias semanas en la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, enfrente de la Real Casa de Correos y sede del Gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid. Esta acampada comenzó con las protestas generadas tras el desahucio de Maricarmen el pasado 26 de septiembre. Ahora, un mes después se produce el desalojo definitivo de la céntrica plaza de Madrid con 334 personas levantadas, la mayor parte en situación de indigencia, cobrándose el operativo con dos personas detenidas por "desobediencia y resistencia a la autoridad". Además, los servicios de limpieza han anunciado que las tiendas de campaña se llevan a los diferentes depósitos municipales y que se les entregarán a quien quiera reclamar su pérdida. El portavoz de la acampada de Sol, Juan Luis Sánchez ha denunciado que el desalojo de la acampada se ha hecho de madrugada y sin avisar a nadie para “pillar a todo el mundo durmiendo” y que ciertos agentes han respondido “con violencia” y él ha sido “gaseado con gas pimienta”. Personalidades se han pronunciado al respecto de esta situación y el alcalde de la ciudad de Madrid lo ha valorado con un mensaje compartido en redes sociales donde destaca el trabajo de los servicios de limpieza de la ciudad. En dicho comunicado, el alcalde ha destacado la cantidad de objetos retirados de la vía pública: “El número de toneladas de residuos recogidas tras el levantamiento de la acampada de Sol asciende a 36,2, un 88,2 % más que lo retirado en la acampada de 2011”. Además, ha agradecido a los servicios municipales de limpieza del ayuntamiento “que llevan trabajando desde esta madrugada para devolver la normalidad a la Puerta del Sol”.
