articles.title: What do I need to bring to vote in Maryland? Election Day guide
articles.summary: If you're heading to vote on Election Day in Maryland, the state has a list of items you are allowed or not allowed to bring with you.
articles.body:
Polls are open in Maryland, but there are a few things eligible voters must know before they visit their polling place.

Most Maryland voters do not need to show identification to vote. However, some first-time voters who registered by mail and did not provide identification when registering may be asked to show ID.

Here's what voters should know about what they should bring, and what they're not allowed to bring.

What do Maryland voters need to bring to their polling place?

The Maryland State Board of Elections says some first-time voters will be asked to show ID before voting.

If you're asked to show ID, you must provide one of the following items: a copy of a current and valid photo ID or a copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other government document that lists your name and address.

Do I need to bring an ID to vote in Maryland?

Most Maryland voters can check in and cast their ballot without showing identification.

ID is generally only required for certain first-time voters who registered by mail and did not provide the necessary identification information when registering.

What can I bring to my Maryland polling place?

You can bring children under 18 with you to vote as long as they do not disrupt or interfere with normal voting procedures.

You're allowed to bring any printed material, including your marked specimen ballot, to help you vote.

Voters can wear clothing, buttons or stickers with political messaging, but they must leave their polling place immediately after voting.

What can't I bring to my Maryland polling place?

Cellphones, cameras, pagers and computer equipment generally cannot be used inside a polling place. There are exceptions for voters using a device to review election information, provide proof of identification or residency, use translation services or take a photo of their marked ballot for personal use before casting it.

Maryland also prohibits firearms inside polling places and within the surrounding restricted electioneering zone, with exceptions for law enforcement.

articles.title: U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at the end of the year, Trump says
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the United States to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel, without providing details.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the United States to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel, without providing details. Oil prices slid in response to Trump’s comments. “Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” he said in a phone interview with “Fox and Friends,” saying that the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.” Trump made the comments while voters were heading to the polls for the midterm elections. During the campaign, U.S. aid to Israel, and Israel’s war in Gaza, have become one of the most contentious issues. On stopping aid, Trump said Israel was “fine with it because, you know, they have become a very successful country,” adding that “they don’t need it.” “Now we’ll help Israel if they need it. You know they’ve been a great ally,” he said, adding that the idea to halt the aid had come from Netanyahu himself. “Can I be honest with you? He brought it up,” Trump added. “He said: ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid,’ because he understands that this is one of their points of contention.” The Israeli prime minister said in January that he hoped to “taper off” American military aid over the next decade. Asked about Trump’s comments Tuesday, a spokesman for Netanyahu said he didn’t know anything about the remarks but would check for details. It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant. A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations have been underway on how Washington’s assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date. In the two years since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli assault on Gaza, the U.S. sent $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to a paper by William D. Hartung, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank based in Washington, D.C. The president appeared to acknowledge a political dimension to the decision, saying, “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.” “I don’t like that because you know it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target,” he said. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump added, referring to Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan progressive Democratic Senate nominee, who has forcefully criticized Israel and U.S. foreign policy during the campaign. Brent crude oil fell by more than 3% to around $101 per barrel, its lowest level in more than three weeks, as investors and traders viewed the comments as potentially further evidence that the Iran war could be ended without escalation. Trump and Netanyahu launched the war on Iran earlier this year, and munitions in the U.S. have been increasingly depleted as a result. The drop added to oil’s biggest one-day decline in three months Monday, after Trump told NBC News that he was not planning to attack Iran after the midterms. The comments were seized upon by Netanyahu’s domestic political opponents. “The cessation of American aid deals a severe blow to Israel’s security and the quality of life in the country,” Yair Golan, head of the left-wing Democrats party, said in a statement. “At a time when Israel’s defense expenditures have reached massive proportions, when Israel needs to replenish its stocks of offensive weaponry, and when air defense capabilities have been eroded following such a prolonged war,” Golan added. “Netanyahu has notched yet another colossal failure to his name.” This is a developing news story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: What time do polls close on Election Day? See list state-by-state
articles.summary: Here's what you need to know about what time polls open and close on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, in your state.
articles.body:
Election Day has arrived as voters are preparing to head to the polls across all 50 states on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Republicans are fighting to keep majorities in both the Senate and U.S. House of Representatives, with key races from Alaska to Texas to Florida being decisive as to whether Democrats can gain control over one or both chambers of Congress.

If you are planning to vote in person, it is important to know where your polling precinct is located and what time it opens. Most states open their polls at 7 a.m. local, but some start voting as early as 5 a.m. or as late as 10 a.m. This information all depends on which state you live in, and sometimes even on your county or municipality. The closing time of your polling precinct also can depend on these factors.

You can check USA TODAY's voter guide or visit Vote.gov and USA.gov for more information on voting and voter registration, which in some states is open through Election Day.

Here is what time polls will open and close in each state, according to states' websites. All times are local.

When do polls open and close for 2026 midterm elections?

Poll opening times can vary by state or municipality. Here is a breakdown by hour of when polls open across the country.

Polls in Alabama are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time on Election Day . Polling places located in the Eastern Time Zone may be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET rather than Central Time.

In Alaska, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., according to the Alaska Division of Elections .

Polls in Arizona are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.

On Election Day, polls in Arkansas are open from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

Polls in California are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

In Colorado, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. in Connecticut.

Polls in Delaware are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Washington DC are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Polls in Florida are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

In Georgia, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. in Hawaii on Election Day.

Most polls are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in Idaho. Some polling places may open at 7 a.m. at the discretion of the county clerk.

Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. in Illinois on Election Day.

In Indiana, polls are open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Iowa are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

State law requires polling places in Kansas to open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. on Election Day. Counties are allowed to open polling locations as early as 6 a.m. and close as late as 8 p.m., however polling locations must be open for at least 12 consecutive hours.

Polls in Kentucky are open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Polls in Louisiana are open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. for Tuesday elections, according to the Louisiana Secretary of State's website .

Voting places in Maine open between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m., depending on the population of the town. All voting places close at 8 p.m. on Election Day, according to the Maine state government's website .

Polls in Maryland are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Most polls in Massachusetts are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., although some municipalities may open polling places as early as 5:45 a.m.

Polls in Michigan are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Minnesota are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day, although municipalities with fewer than 500 residents may open polling places as late as 10 a.m.

In Mississippi, polling places are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Missouri are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Most polls in Montana are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Polling places with fewer than 400 registered voters who intend to vote in person must remain open from at least noon until 8 p.m., or until all registered voters have voted, at which point the polling place must close immediately.

Polling places located in the Central time zone are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., while polling places located in the Mountain time zone are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Polls in Nevada are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Hours for polling places in New Hampshire vary by municipality, however polls must open by 11 a.m. and cannot close before 7 p.m.

Polling places in New Jersey are open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

In New Mexico, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in New York are open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.

Polling locations in North Carolina are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

Polls in North Dakota open between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m. and close between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m.

Polling locations in Ohio are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Oklahoma are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

In Oregon, polling locations are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. in Pennsylvania.

Most polling locations in Rhode Island are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., with one exception – polls in New Shoreham open at 9 a.m.

Polling locations in South Carolina are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in South Dakota are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Polling location hours vary by county in Tennessee, however all polling places close 8 p.m. ET. Polls must be open for a minimum of 10 consecutive hours, but not more than 13 hours.

Polls in Texas are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Polling locations in Utah are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Polling locations in Vermont open between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.

Polls in Virginia are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Opening hours for polling locations in Washington vary by municipality, however all polls close at 8 p.m.

Polls in West Virginia are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

Polling locations in Wisconsin are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.

Polls in Wyoming are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

articles.title: Michigan voters weigh in after Dem Rep Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate
articles.summary: Michigan Republican Mike Rogers' campaign touted Haley Stevens' endorsement as a breakthrough with Black and Jewish voters before Election Day.
articles.body: OAKLAND COUNTY, MICHIGAN — Michigan’s Republican ticket had a clear message for voters preparing to vote in the midterm elections: Their path to victory relies on winning over voters who typically don’t align themselves with the GOP. That prospect appeared to be buoyed by Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th-hour endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed. Early Monday afternoon, Republican operatives in Michigan blasted out a press release advertising an event just hours later intended to tout Stevens’ endorsement and its purported impact on Black and Jewish voters. In front of a throng of press at the Michigan GOP’s headquarters, six community leaders representing African Americans and Jews criticized what they saw as El-Sayed’s excesses and lauded Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers. Broadly, they argued that El-Sayed had insufficiently distanced himself from some of his radical associations, that Stevens' endorsement had real significance for the race and that they were seeing an unprecedented groundswell of support for Republicans among their peers. MIKE ROGERS DISHES ON HOW SHOCK HALEY STEVENS ENDORSEMENT UNFOLDED HOURS BEFORE ELECTION DAY In addition to the community leaders, close to two dozen others — many of whom were Black or Jewish — attended the event as well. While some political observers have cast doubt on the impact of Stevens' endorsement and the degree to which African Americans and Jews are defecting from the Democratic Party, members of those communities told Fox News Digital the shift is happening. "I believe it's going to make a big difference that she came out," Michelle Nard, an African American former Democrat running for state Senate, told Fox News Digital. "She had a big following. She's a great congresswoman, a great state representative for the United States." BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’ Nard recounted how she had recently spoken to a Black woman who highlighted that her community makes a big deal of going to the polls on Election Day, a point she used to stress that Haley’s endorsement, though late in the cycle, could still influence last-second voters. "You have strong Haley Stevens supporters in our community that will support her to the end, and then you have some that feel betrayed," Marcus Bowman, a metro Detroit school board trustee, told Fox News Digital. Bowman, who says he knows Stevens personally, said: "True supporters of Haley Stevens, they know her as a person and they know what she represents. I think they will follow her and respect her for her decision based off some of the radical things we've heard about Abdul El-Sayed." While those who spoke were handpicked for a Republican news conference, there is some data to back up Black voter defection. Between August and September, El-Sayed’s support among African Americans held steady at around 75%, well below the party's typical benchmark. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS The Arab American community in the Detroit metropolitan area has historically been at odds with African Americans in the areas across a number of issues, a theme that has come up occasionally during El-Sayed’s campaign. While comparable polls have not found similar trends among Jewish voters, who are a much smaller part of Michigan’s electorate, a number of high-profile members of the communities, including top donors, have flocked to the Rogers camp. "Haley, what she did was give a lot of Jews permission, hardcore left-wing Democrats, permission to now say, you know what, if Haley can endorse him, I can vote for him," Aaron Tobin, a conservative Jewish community leader, told Fox News Digital in reference to Mike Rogers. "Now I think she's broken that wall down, and now they can see that a hardcore Democrat — and she was very successful and very popular in Michigan — if she said Mike Rogers is good enough for her, I think a lot of Jews are going to say, 'I'm going to vote for him because Abdul just says the worst things.'" Ezra, another Jewish voter, told Fox News Digital that he believes Jews have increasingly been abandoned by the Democratic Party and, even if Stevens’ endorsement doesn’t move the needle, he’s grateful that she took a stand. "The [March 12] terrorist attack in [a] West Bloomfield [synagogue], I believe was the starting point of the Detroit Jewish community being afraid and that fear was not alleviated over the next [six months]. That fear has not been alleviated by Abdul El-Sayed in any sort of way, which is why I think you're seeing this," he said. "We're waiting for something and it's not coming. And so that's why I think you're seeing so many in the Jewish community moving for Mike Rogers because they're like, you know what, that guy's going to keep my family safe. The other guy's not." MAMDANI, HASAN PIKER AMONG RADICAL LEFT-WING VOICES ERUPTING OVER HALEY STEVENS' ENDORSEMENT SWITCH "I think in some ways, it's, it's more brave because it's at the last minute. In some ways, you know what, who knows, even if it, if it's 100 votes or 1000 votes, then it makes a difference," he added. These alleged breakthroughs with traditionally Democratic constituencies took center stage at Rogers’ closing rally on Monday night. At one point, the campaign invited six Black and Jewish voters, most of them former Democrats, to take the stage where they explained why they believed El-Sayed to be too extreme for their support. Rogers himself praised the group during his final campaign speech, invoked the need for unity and thanked Stevens at length for her endorsement. Conservatives at the rally were clearly grateful to Stevens for her endorsement, with nearly every mention of her name being met with cheers or chants of her name. Republicans are even optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement could trickle down to their down-ballot races. MICHIGAN DEM CLAIMS STEVENS SHOT DOWN ROGERS ENDORSEMENT RUMOR HOURS BEFORE TURNING ON EL-SAYED "I was on the ground last week in Michigan and Ohio, and the momentum in Michigan is real. It was real before Haley Stevens endorsed Mike Rogers, even more real now," Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, told Fox News Digital. Piper said he "absolutely" believes Stevens’ endorsement will move the needle for Michigan Republican attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd. "You know, around the Detroit area, Grosse Pointe, Detroit, elsewhere, I saw homemade yard signs in the yards of Black churches that said African Americans and Jews stand together. And that was powerful." Lloyd said he is optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers could give him a boost. "Well, I saw something today in the news that basically said 50% of the available voters have voted through absentee and early voting. We still have one day left. And as we've said, you know, the race isn't done until 8 o'clock tomorrow night when the polls close," he said. "So, if this made a difference for someone who had been sitting on the sideline and they decided they were going to get out and vote because of it, I'm excited for that." Democrats have argued Stevens’ endorsement could strengthen, rather than weaken, El-Sayed’s support. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said he expected the episode to galvanize Democrats, while El-Sayed’s campaign reported raising $2.4 million Sunday, its largest fundraising day of the campaign. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While cutting into the Democratic Party’s margins by successfully pulling away Black and Jewish voters could prove valuable to the GOP, a reversion among Arab voters — who swung toward Republicans in 2024 but strongly favor El-Sayed — could erase such gains. Fox News’ final power ranking rated Michigan’s Senate race as a toss-up, meaning that, as voters head to the polls, neither party holds a clear edge.

articles.title: The economy is on the ballot. 3 charts reveal the reality voters face as they head to the polls
articles.summary: Inflation outpacing wages, gas prices above $4, and mortgage rates past 7% are squeezing voters even as the S&P 500 surges over 26% under Trump.
articles.body: Voters who have already cast ballots and those heading to the polls on Tuesday are weighing an economy shaped by rising everyday costs, surging home prices and strong gains in the stock market. President Donald Trump vowed a better economy and a brighter financial future in his 2024 bid for office. But nearly two years into his second term, fuel prices have surged, inflation has accelerated and buying a home remains expensive — all pressures that put Republicans' affordability promises to the test in this midterm election cycle. Three charts help exhibit the economic forces shaping voters’ choices as control of Congress hangs in the balance and the future of Trump's agenda is put on the line. HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS Everyday costs keep climbing The latest inflation report showed consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year through September and 0.6% from August. The Consumer Price Index tracks prices across a broad range of household expenses, including food, housing, medical care and transportation. Trade policy has added to some of those costs. A New York Federal Reserve study found that Trump's tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods researchers examined. Roughly one-third of the increase came from U.S.-made products, as domestic manufacturers faced higher costs for imported materials and components under Trump's agenda. The impact varies by household, but these figures offer a snapshot of the price pressures voters may weigh ahead of the midterms. They show how costs have changed, though not how voters will assign responsibility. Diesel costs ripple through the economy Higher energy costs are putting pressure on households and businesses, as the wars in Iran and Ukraine disrupt global fuel supplies. Diesel prices have climbed sharply, rising from about $3.45 per gallon in early 2025 to a peak of $6.53 in October 2026, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The increase matters beyond the pump because trucks, freight trains and farm equipment rely on diesel. AMERICAN-MADE GOODS ALSO GOT MORE EXPENSIVE UNDER TRUMP TARIFFS, NEW RESEARCH FINDS Higher fuel costs can raise expenses for businesses moving groceries, packages and building materials, which may absorb some of the increase or pass it along to customers. Gasoline prices are also adding to household costs. They jumped 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s overall increase in the Consumer Price Index. A tougher path to homeownership Housing remains a major affordability challenge, particularly for prospective buyers. Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.24% as of Oct. 29, while the latest median price for an existing home was $417,500 in September, according to the National Association of Realtors. Mortgage rates shape buyers’ monthly payments, and home prices determine how much they need to borrow, making it harder for many households to enter the market. TRUMP’S HOUSING CHIEF PAINTS A GRIM PICTURE FOR HOMEOWNERSHIP IN ONE MAJOR AMERICAN CITY Rising home values can benefit people who already own property, but that wealth is difficult to access without selling or borrowing against a home. For renters and first-time buyers, the costs are more immediate. The data offer a snapshot of the costs voters have faced, but the charts alone cannot show how they will weigh the economy — or which party they will hold responsible — as results come in.

articles.title: Midterms 2026: Will Republicans or Democrats win control of the House? These are the key races to watch.
articles.summary: Democrats are playing offense. Republicans are playing defense. But the GOP also has certain advantages it didn't have in the past.
articles.body:
It's Election Day in America. Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives are delivering their closing messages to voters — and hoping they can help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3.

The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) .

Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top.

The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% of those contests (representing 346 seats) are not considered competitive.

House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison.

As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 18 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 18 "lean Democratic," and 18 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 18 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 17 seats where the same could be said about Republicans.

That's 89 competitive districts — again, out of 435.

It's clear from looking at those ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Only 31 Democratic-held seats are considered competitive, and more than half of them (17) are "likely" to remain Democratic, according to Cook. Just four Democratic seats are toss-ups. Just three are leaning Republican.

In contrast, a full 58 Republican-held seats are considered competitive — and about half of them are toss-ups (14) or leaning Democratic (13).

Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 .

On Monday, Cook shifted another five of its race ratings toward Democrats — part of a pattern that has seen the outlet move a total of 80 race ratings toward Democrats over the last few weeks.

"As the House battleground map has expanded, Democrats now have the potential to win their largest majority since 2009. President Donald Trump's approval rating is underwater even in deep red seats that he won comfortably in 2024, and heavy spending from Republicans doesn't appear to be moving the needle," Cook's House analyst recently wrote . "While Democrats won't reach the 257 seats they had following President Barack Obama's election — a high water mark for them this century — they could surpass the majorities they had following the 2006 and 2018 blue wave cycles."

She went on to project that Democrats "will flip 12 to 25 seats, giving them as many as 240 seats in the House."

Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which means more paths to a House majority.

Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House.

So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats.

Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House.

The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right.

Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , an average of 59% of Americans currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -21% — near his all-time low.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 70% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 45-point gap.

Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of 9 percentage points , on average.

Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has expanded as swing voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic.

To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. On Election Day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House.

If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again.

But are the polls right? Recently, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment.

They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver .

The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was.

Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day.

This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states .

Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3.

After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver .

Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans.

Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). If that plays out, it would net the GOP four seats overall.

It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing.

The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority.

articles.title: Will Republicans or Democrats win control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms? These are key races to watch.
articles.summary: The GOP's majority is on the line as Democrats look to flip seats in a handful of historically red states.
articles.body:
Control of both chambers of Congress is up for grabs today. But as important as the House of Representatives is, all signs point to the true drama of the midterms being in the battle for the Senate.

There are 35 Senate seats on the ballot this year. Most of those races won't be competitive. The balance of power in the Senate will be decided by the dozen or so states where the outcome truly is uncertain. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, which means they can lose three seats and still maintain control of the chamber — thanks to Vice President JD Vance's constitutionally granted power to break ties in an evenly split Senate.

Forecasters widely expect Democrats to flip the House, but view the Senate as a "true toss-up."

The key Senate battlegrounds include traditional swing states, idiosyncratic areas of the Northeast and historically Republican states where Democrats have rarely been competitive in recent elections.

The outcome will have enormous implications for the final two years of President Trump's tenure in the White House. Democrats only need to gain control of one chamber to have the power to block or reshape Trump's legislative agenda. But a Senate majority would empower them to do much more. They would have an effective veto over Trump's nominees for high-ranking Cabinet positions and could block him from appointing any new Supreme Court justices. Control over key Senate committees would also allow Democrats to launch sweeping investigations into Trump and his administration.

Here's a rundown of the races that will likely decide which party controls the Senate after the midterms.

True to the state's image, there's a wildness to Alaska's Senate race that you won't find elsewhere in the country. On paper, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan should be well-positioned to win a third term in the Senate. Alaska is a consistently red state that has only elected a Democrat to the Senate once in the past 45 years. Democrats' challenges in the state have been so acute recently that they didn't even have a candidate on the ballot the last time Sullivan was up for reelection.

But forecasters expect this year's race to be much closer. Sullivan's main opponent is former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola , who was Alaska's lone member of the House from 2022 to 2025. Peltola, the first Alaska Native and first woman to represent the Last Frontier in Congress, is a rare Democrat with a record of success in statewide elections.

The race suddenly received a surge in national attention after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit on Oct. 22 to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan suffers a close loss, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant whose purpose is to confuse voters and siphon away votes. The New York Times later reported that operatives aligned with Peltola helped recruit the second Sullivan to run. Peltola denied any involvement in the alleged plot. The lawsuit was dismissed by a federal judge in Alaska on Sunday; however, the DOJ said it plans to appeal that decision. Some congressional Republicans have also suggested that Peltola should not be allowed to be seated in the Senate if she wins.

It would likely take a major blue wave election for incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody to be at a real risk of being unseated by progressive Democrat Angie Nixon. The GOP has won the last two Senate races in Florida by an average of 14 points. Polls have shown Nixon trailing by a smaller margin than that, but still far enough behind for forecasters to rate the race as favoring Republicans.

On top of flipping a handful of GOP-held seats, Democrats' chances of gaining control of the Senate rely on keeping the ones they already have. One of the most important is in Georgia.

Sen. Jon Ossoff became a rising star within the Democratic Party when he pulled off a stunning upset in the 2020 elections, defeating incumbent Republican David Perdue in an extremely tight runoff. Ossoff is now running for reelection for the first time. His opponent is Rep. Mike Collins, a MAGA-friendly congressman who has created controversy with a series of divisive social media posts during his tenure in the House.

More recently, Collins has faced intense scrutiny over his social media posts and the online activity of people close to him , including his son-in-law .

Polls have shown Ossoff with a healthy lead over Collins, enough of a gap that forecasters at the non-partisan Center for Politics wrote in July that it would be a "true shock" if he isn't reelected.

It wasn't that long ago that Iowa was viewed as one of the country's quintessential swing states, but the Hawkeye State has shifted significantly to the right over the past decade — to the point where it's no longer competitive in presidential elections.

That said, polls suggest Democrats appear to have a real chance of flipping the Senate seat held by retiring incumbent Joni Ernst. Their nominee is Josh Turek, a state lawmaker and two-time Paralympic gold medalist. A moderate who describes himself as a "prairie populist," Turek has focused heavily on how Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran have affected farmers in his state throughout the campaign.

His opponent is GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former local news anchor who cruised to the Republican nomination after earning Trump's endorsement. Polling of the race has fluctuated significantly, with both candidates showing small leads at different times.

It has been almost 100 years since Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate, but the state may be in play this year as incumbent Republican Roger Marshall looks to keep the GOP's nearly century-long winning streak alive.

His opponent is Adam Hamilton, a pastor and the founder of the nation's largest United Methodist church. Polls in the final weeks of the campaign have mostly shown Hamilton ahead. Libertarian Party candidate David Graham is also on the ballot and has drawn a small but potentially significant share of support in some polls.

Democrats have been eyeing Sen. Susan Collins's seat for decades, but the Republican has fended off every challenger they've sent her way during her 30 years in the Senate. Her opponent this time around will be Troy Jackson , a former logger and longtime member of the state legislature. Jackson was chosen at a hastily planned convention after the party's original nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault, which he denied, among other controversies.

Collins has historically managed to outperform other Republicans when she's been on the ballot, even in "blue wave" years like 2020, in part because of her longstanding reputation as a relative moderate within her party. But that image is being tested in this race. Jackson has centered much of his campaign on tying Collins to some of the more high-profile times she's sided with the president on major issues, particularly her votes to confirm Supreme Court justices who later joined the majority in overturning Roe v. Wade .

Jackson faces his own challenges. He has been playing catch-up after becoming the nominee so late in the process. He will also face scrutiny over his past conservative positions on issues like abortion and same-sex marriage, which are a far cry from the progressive political views he expresses today.

One of the nation's few genuine swing states is home to one of the most pivotal midterm matchups. Incumbent Democrat Gary Peters opted not to run for a third term, setting the stage for a nail-biter of a Democratic primary in which progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, a relative moderate, in a major victory for the party's left wing. There was far less drama on the Republican side, where former Rep. Mike Rogers cruised to the GOP nomination.

Rogers was also the Republican nominee in 2024, losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by 0.34 percentage points of the vote in one of the tightest Senate races in the country. El-Sayed, who supports policies like a billionaire's tax and Medicare for All, will need the support of centrist Democrats and swing voters in order to build a big enough coalition to win. Polls have shown El-Sayed in front late in the race, but with margins small enough to make a win by Rogers entirely plausible. It's unclear how a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, might shift the race in its final stages.

Incumbent Sen. Tina Smith has opted not to run for a second term, which could help create an opening for Republicans to break Democrats' longstanding hold on Minnesota's U.S. Senate delegation.

To pursue that goal, the GOP has enlisted a rare political newcomer with widespread name recognition: Former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya. Her Democratic opponent is Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

The race so far has been defined by the remarkably different approaches of the two candidates. Tafoya has worked to push her party toward the political center, portraying herself as a moderate Republican and mostly focusing on issues like affordability and public safety while steering clear of some of the more divisive parts of Trump's agenda. Flanagan, on the other hand, is a progressive who represents a significant step to the left on policy for Democrats relative to Smith.

Polls have shown Flanagan leading by a few points in the late stages of the race.

In a state as red as Nebraska, rather than fielding their own candidate to challenge incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, Democrats have thrown their support behind independent candidate Dan Osborn.

This is the second time that Osborn, a Navy veteran and former labor union leader, has run for the Senate in a race without a Democratic candidate. Two years ago, he finished about 6 points behind GOP Sen. Deb Fisher in the state's closest Senate race in more than two decades.

Osborn has been deeply critical of both parties and says he opposes parts of the Democratic Party's platform. But if he's elected, the GOP would lose a Senate seat it currently holds and one vote that it can comfortably count on in support of Trump's legislative agenda.

The Granite State is rarely discussed as a swing state because it consistently votes for Democrats in presidential elections. But Senate races are a different story. Several Republicans have been elected to represent New Hampshire in the Senate in recent decades. One of them is John Sununu, who is running to regain the seat he lost in 2008 when he was defeated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring incumbent. Sununu is part of a political dynasty in the state. His father, also named John, and his brother Chris both served as governor.

The Democratic nominee is Rep. Chris Pappas, a moderate who comfortably outpaced a democratic socialist rival in his party's primary. Pappas is the first gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress and would become the first openly gay male senator in U.S. history if he is elected.

If polls are accurate, Republicans have a lot of ground to make up if they want to hold on to this seat from the Tarheel State. Incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis, a rare member of the GOP caucus to defy the president in some circumstances, has opted not to seek reelection. The Republican nominee to replace him is Michael Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee.

Whatley has a strong history in North Carolina, having run the state Republican Party for nearly five years, but he lacks the statewide name recognition of his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper.

Both of Cooper's gubernatorial wins were reasonably close, but polls have shown him with a significant lead over Whatley. Forecasters have also shifted the race toward Democrats.

The Buckeye State has trended to the right over the past decade or so, but a unique set of circumstances has contributed to making this race a genuine toss-up in the eyes of some forecasters. Aside from the Democratic and Republican nominees, Libertarian William Redpath and Greg Levy of the Party for Socialism and Liberation are also on the ballot. These two lesser-known candidates are getting as much as 6% of voters' support in polls, collectively, which is potentially enough to influence the outcome in a very tight race.

Husted is the rare incumbent with less experience than his challenger. He has only been in the Senate since 2025, when he was appointed to fill the vacancy created when JD Vance became vice president. Brown, on the other hand, served three full terms in the Senate before losing his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown also has a massive cash advantage, which has allowed his campaign to spend more than four times as much as Husted's so far, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Despite all of that, Brown is still swimming upstream in a state that has become solidly red over the past few election cycles.

The word "competitive" is rarely used to describe statewide races in a place as red as South Carolina, but the death of longtime incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham in July has set up what could be the Palmetto State's first tight Senate race in a generation.

Graham's sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to finish the rest of his term and is now running for a full six-year term. Her opponent is Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who has staked out several policy positions that reflect the state's conservatism, including support for the Second Amendment, tax cuts and strong immigration enforcement.

Republicans have comfortably won every Senate election in South Carolina since the early 2000s, but Trump's declining approval rating in the state and apparent concerns about Graham's lack of experience have likely contributed to making this a much closer race. Recent polls have shown Andrews trailing by as little as a single point, though forecasters still list the state as a leaning in Republican's direction.

Republicans haven't lost a statewide election in the Lone Star State in more than three decades, but forecasters say Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico has a chance of ending that streak in November.

His Republican opponent is Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a tightly contested and often contentious Republican primary. Paxton has faced serious legal issues during his tenure as Texas's top law enforcement official, including accusations of corruption that led the state House to impeach him in 2023. The state Senate later acquitted him on all articles it considered.

Polls have consistently shown a tight contest , with a good number finding Talarico leading by a small margin.

articles.title: Abortion, transgender rights and voter ID: These are the major 2026 midterms ballot measures voters will decide
articles.summary: Ballot measures voters a way to directly alter their state laws, rather than relying solely on legislators to create policy on their behalf.
articles.body:
The battle for control of Congress is getting the lion's share of the attention in the lead-up to the midterms, but there are a lot of other consequential measures that'll appear on ballots today that could have a direct impact on voters' lives.

Ballot measures often don't receive much national attention, but every two years, voters across the country decide whether to adopt policies that have major implications for their states. This year is no different.

There are more than 140 total measures collectively across 40 states this year. Many touch on some of the biggest issues in U.S. politics, including abortion, transgender rights, voting and the democratic process itself.

Ballot measures can give the people a way to directly alter the laws in their states instead of relying solely on their elected representatives to create policy on their behalf. In some cases, they provide an opportunity for voters to endorse or reject something their state legislature wants to do. In other cases, regular citizens can get their preferred policy on the ballot directly through a signature-gathering campaign.

Here's a rundown of some of the major measures on statewide ballots this year.

The Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the nationwide abortion protections established by Roe v. Wade instantly turned abortion access into a state-by-state issue. It also led to a flurry of ballot measures across the country in which voters were asked to decide whether their states should protect or restrict abortion rights. In the years since, voters have generally come down in favor of protecting abortion rights.

That trend will get another test this year due to abortion-related measures in four states.

In Idaho , voters will decide whether to overturn their state's strict abortion restrictions and establish a right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including abortion until fetal viability. If the measure passes, Idaho will become the latest red state where voters have used a ballot initiative to expand abortion rights.

One of those red states is Missouri , where voters approved a measure in 2024 that struck down some of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws. A Republican-backed measure on this year's ballot would repeal that 2024 amendment and allow strict abortion restrictions to be put back into place. The same measure would also create new limits on gender-affirming care in the state.

Two other states that already have relatively permissive laws around abortion access — Nevada and Virginia — are voting on measures that would enshrine abortion rights in their state constitutions, a step that would make it much harder to restrict access in the future.

The debate over transgender rights, particularly when it comes to minors, has become a central issue in American politics. It should be no surprise, then, that a number of states have measures related to the topic on the ballot this year. All of them would impose new limits on transgender rights.

Four states — Washington , Nebraska , Arizona and Colorado — will vote on measures that would ban trans athletes from participating on sports teams that match their gender identity. There are some important differences from state to state, though. The proposals in Washington and Nebraska would only apply to girls' and women's teams. Colorado's and Arizona's would apply to both male and female teams.

Washington's bill also includes a stipulation that would require all K-12 students, whether they identify as trans or not, who want to play girls' or women's sports to have their sex verified by a doctor . Arizona's measure would also ban schools from allowing trans minors or adults to access bathrooms, locker rooms or other private spaces designated for a sex that doesn't match the one they were assigned at birth.

A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. Missouri's measure would go even further. In addition to banning the surgeries, it would also prohibit minors from receiving other forms of gender-affirming care, like hormone therapy and puberty blockers.

Six states will vote on measures related to voter ID.

Those in California, Colorado and Nevada would either establish or expand laws requiring voters to show ID when they cast their ballots. Each of the proposals would also require voter ID for mail-in ballots.

Arizona, Ohio and North Carolina already have strict voter ID requirements in place under state law, but measures in each state would add or expand those requirements in their state constitutions.

Schools have been a major flash point for culture war battles in recent years. A handful of measures on the ballot in November will ask voters to weigh in on some of those debates.

Arizona and Wisconsin both have measures that would ban affirmative action in schools and all other government agencies.

Alabama has a pair of proposals. One would require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week. The other would make the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance a daily requirement and mandate school boards to adopt policies that allow student-led prayer.

A sweeping parental rights initiative in Washington would give parents of public school students substantially more oversight over the education their children receive, including the power to review curricula and textbooks. It would also put strict new limits on the kinds of medical care schools can provide without parental notification and roll back changes to the state's parental rights law that protected against discrimination and bullying in schools.

Ballot measures frequently center on contentious political issues, but in recent years, the initiative process itself has increasingly become the subject of political debate.

Five states will vote on measures that would make it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law. They would accomplish that by either raising the share of the vote certain measures need to get approved or restricting the subjects that initiatives can address.

Voters in California and Utah will consider measures that would require certain initiatives that would raise taxes to receive more than the simple majority of support they currently need to be successful. California's would raise the bar for voter-proposed local special taxes to two-thirds of the vote. Utah's would set the new standard for tax-related citizen initiatives at 60%. North Dakota and South Dakota both have measures that would require any attempt to change their state constitutions to get 60% of the vote.

Changing the threshold for success by 10 percentage points may not sound like a huge deal, but it is often the difference between a proposal becoming law and being rejected. For example, initiatives in Florida that would have legalized abortion and recreational marijuana use both received majority support from voters in 2024, but neither became law because they fell short of the state's 60% approval standard.

Idaho has a measure on the ballot that would ban initiatives aimed at legalizing marijuana, psychedelics and other narcotics. If it passes, only the state legislature would have the power to legalize or decriminalize those substances.

Another two states will decide on measures designed to protect the initiative process. A proposal in Montana would amend the state's constitution to guarantee citizens' rights to pursue ballot initiatives and make it harder for the government to interfere with measures approved by voters.

In Missouri , voters will weigh in on a measure that would prohibit the state's Republican-led legislature from weakening the initiative process. It would also bar it from amending or repealing any measures that have passed unless 80% of both chambers agree to put the change before voters.

There are many pivotal ballot initiatives being considered across the country that don't fit neatly into a specific category. Here are a few of them.

Alaska voters will decide whether to repeal their state's recently adopted ranked-choice voting system. A proposal in Arizona would ban new traffic cameras without direct voter approval. Nebraska will choose whether to legalize online sports betting . Vermont will consider a measure that would ban discrimination based on gender identity. Virginia will decide if people convicted of felonies should have their right to vote restored once they're released from prison. A measure in Wisconsin would prohibit the government from closing places of worship during public health emergencies. Massachusetts will consider whether recreational marijuana sales should once again be made illegal. A proposal on the ballot in North Dakota would require all public schools to provide free breakfast and lunch.

Lower-stakes — but still noteworthy — measures under consideration include a Colorado initiative that would enshrine the right to hunt and fish in the state constitution and a request for Idaho voters to select an official state gun .

articles.title: Trump says US will stop providing aid to Israel after year-end
articles.summary: The president accuses Democrats of weaponising US aid to Israel as a "talking point" with which to attack Republicans.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said the US will stop providing funding to Israel at the end of the year, following a deal he struck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In a telephone interview with Fox News on Tuesday morning, Trump said that a deal had been reached "months ago" that will see the US stop providing $4bn (£2.98bn) each year.

"We've ⁠already agreed that ⁠by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel," Trump said. ‌"Now we'll help Israel if they need it."

It is unclear what funds the president was referring to, although a memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8bn a year in military assistance to Israel expires at the end of 2028.

The BBC has contacted the White House for clarification. The Israeli Prime Minister's office has yet to comment.

Speaking to Fox News, Trump said that Israel no longer needs American funding.

"As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," he said.

He also accused Democrats of weaponising US assistance to Israel as a "talking point" with which to attack Republicans.

Trump said that Israel can purchase weapons from the US if necessary. The contours of any new procurement or investment arrangement to help Israel's military remain unclear.

In a May interview with CBS, the BBC's US partner, Prime Minister Netanyahu said he wants to "draw down" US financial support to Israel "to zero" from the annual $3.8bn the country receives.

"Let's start now and do it over the next decade, over the next ten years, but I want to start now," he said. "I don't want to wait for the next Congress. I want to start now."

Israel has been the largest recipient of US foreign assistance since the end of the Second World War.

A Congressional report published last year put the total price tag at $174bn, non-inflation-adjusted.

The US-Israel relationship still has substantial bipartisan backing, but support has been softening among Democrats, particularly following the start of the war in Gaza in October 2023.

In July, Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie forced a vote on a bill to cut $3.3bn in security aid to Israel and he received support from 103 Democrats in the chamber. He was the only Republican to support the amendment. The measure was defeated by 314 votes to 104.

A September poll conducted by Quinnipiac University found that nearly half - 48% - of voters believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% in 2017.

Among Democrats, the figure stands at 67%, compared to 17% for Republicans.

articles.title: Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?
articles.summary: In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.
articles.body: In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect. Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term. Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time. Of course, no one, including the Decision Desk, will know what will unfold until election night, but we will have a good sense possibly early in the night of how the contests are trending. The answer of when we could call control in both the House and Senate depends not only on how states count their votes, but on how close the races will be. When we could know Senate control Senate control will likely come down to the eight races that NBC News rates as either toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas) or lean Democratic (Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire). Assuming that Democrats win the states NBC News currently rates as “Likely” Democratic (which includes flipping North Carolina’s Senate seat from red to blue, and keeping Georgia in their column), Democrats still need to win five of these eight contests. Some of these states are quick to count their ballots, and others are perennially slow. If some of these Senate contests are as close as we expect, calling control of the Senate as a whole could take us into the early morning hours of Wednesday, regardless of who wins those individual races. It is also a real possibility that Americans will wake up at a slightly more reasonable hour on Wednesday without a majority decided, even if we have a good sense of who will ultimately win. And if Senate control comes down to the outcome in Alaska, we’ll all be here awhile. In that case, it will take a couple of weeks to know who won the majority thanks to the state’s ranked choice voting system. Past elections offer a useful guide to how quickly we expect to see votes counted in each of these states, even if the timing Tuesday night is not exact. Let’s look more closely at each of these categories — the fast-counting states, the slow-but-steady states, and the ranked choice wild cards. The fast counters Votes in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas were counted fairly quickly in 2024. We expect over 80% of the vote in those states to be counted by midnight Eastern time. If those historical patterns hold, there is a good chance that those Senate races will be called. And some of these calls may come in before midnight if there is some spread in the races as some recent polls suggest. But Democrats must win five of these battleground Senate races to take a majority, which means that even if they win all four states here, NBC News would still not be able to project control of the Senate. The steady counters In two of the key battleground states, New Hampshire and Michigan, nearly all votes will be counted over the course of election night, but more steadily and slowly than the fast counters. Here, elections are administered by towns and municipalities, not by counties. This results in a more decentralized and variable counting process that lasts until early morning, or even midday Wednesday. How quickly these races are called really depends upon the margin of the race. Earlier in the election cycle, polls suggested both these races would be close. Recent polls favoring the Democratic candidates and what appears to be a Democratic advantage in the early vote in Michigan mean there’s a wide range of timing possibilities there. If the nationwide Democratic momentum translates to results, New Hampshire could possibly be called before midnight. But that seems to be highly unlikely in a place like Michigan, where Wayne County, home to Detroit, often releases large batches of votes between midnight and 3 a.m. ET. This is such a significant source of ballots that statewide races in Michigan often cannot be called without Wayne County’s results. The takeaway here is that if the Senate races in these states are close as the polls have indicated all along, it’s unlikely that calls will come before the early morning hours. But it all depends upon how far apart the two candidates are in the state, and we won’t know that until tonight. The ranked choice states Maine and Alaska are the slowest counters of the group. As in New Hampshire, Maine’s elections are administered by towns, each with their own schedule for tabulating ballots and releasing results. In Alaska, mail ballots from remote corners of the state can arrive up to 15 days after the election. If these historical patterns hold, there will not be enough votes counted on election night to call a close race in either state. In 2024, the presidential race in Maine was called on Wednesday at 4:40 p.m. ET, and in Alaska on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points, while Trump won Alaska by 13 points. It’s possible the margins in this year’s Senate contests could be much closer. There is a second complication in Maine and Alaska that could cause even more delay in knowing which party will control the Senate. These states both use ranked choice voting for their Senate races, in which voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of more than 50% of voters, the winner will be determined by ranked choice tabulation, in which the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their votes are reallocated based on voters’ next-most preferred candidates. In Alaska, the ranked choice tabulation occurs 15 days after Election Day. Maine does not provide official guidelines on when its ranked choice tabulation will occur, but in June, the ranked choice results were released 10 days after Maine’s primary election. In either case, if one or both of these seats are needed to win a majority, we may not know until the next day, or even for several weeks, which party will control the Senate. What about the House? Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to flip control of the House, and they’re heavily favored to succeed. But the size of that majority depends on how much voters shift their support toward the Democrats and away from Republicans. A recent NBC News Decision Desk analysis shows evidence that this nationwide shift could be big enough to produce a historically large majority for the Democrats — or it could be sufficiently small that either party could end up with a razor-thin majority. (The House is made up of 435 seats, all up for re-election every two years, and 218 seats are needed for control.) The size of that majority for either party matters significantly to our ability to project control of the chamber. The smaller the final size of the majority, the longer it will take for the Decision Desk to be certain of who will control the House. If current polls are overestimating Democratic support and the size of the House majority for either party is small, the 2022 and 2024 elections provide some idea of timing. During the 2022 midterms, it took the NBC News Decision Desk eight days after Election Day to project that Republicans would win a slim majority. This call came as the Decision Desk projected the Republicans would win California’s 27th District, their 218th win. The ultimate size of their majority was nine seats. In the 2024 election, the Republicans won an even smaller majority — just five seats. This election also took until the second Wednesday after Election Day for the Decision Desk to project the 218th seat for the Republicans. If the size of the Democrats’ or Republicans’ majority this year is a single-digit number of seats, we expect it to take days or weeks for either party to reach 218 seats. Just like the Senate elections, the House elections in Maine and Alaska use ranked choice voting to determine a winner. If control of the House hinges on Maine’s 2nd District or Alaska’s lone district, we may have to wait until ranked choice tabulation occurs 10 to 15 days after Election Day. On the other hand, if current polls end up being close to accurate, Democrats would be poised to win at least 230 seats, according to the recent Decision Desk analysis. This could speed up when we know control. Throughout the night, the NBC News Decision Desk uses a statistical model to estimate the total number of seats that the Democrats and Republicans will end up winning. It is possible that NBC News will report this estimate on election night. The House model relies on past and current vote counts; it does not use any polling, including exit polls, in its estimation. Early House indicators with clues for timing Elections in states with early polling close times or that count their ballots quickly can also provide an indication of where things may end up. Kentucky’s 6th District, which Trump won in 2024 by 15 points, is a good example of an early bellwether district. The Republican-held district has its polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and in 2024 it reported nearly 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. While the Democrats do not need their candidate, Zach Dembo, to win this district to earn a majority, a low-single-digit win by the Republican candidate, Ralph Alvarado, is a favorable signal for the Democrats’ chances of winning the House. If Dembo were to win this district, it would likely foretell a Democratic tsunami, as there are 267 districts nationwide where Trump performed more poorly on his way to the White House. And if Alvarado were to win by a margin close to or in the double digits, it may suggest that neither party will end up with a large majority. Florida, which tends to report its votes quickly, also has several congressional districts worth paying attention to early in the night. One of these is Florida’s 25th, where Democrat Jared Moskowitz seeks re-election in a district that Florida Republicans redrew to favor Trump by 9 points. If Moskowitz loses to Republican Scott Singer, it would be a major victory for Republicans and may foreshadow the party holding on to House control. If Moskowitz wins comfortably, it may signal a large Democratic wave. Florida’s 14th District and Florida’s 22nd District are also Democratic-held toss-ups that Republicans redrew to be districts Trump would have won by 10.5 points. Given how quickly Florida counts its ballots, these two districts may be the first toss-ups NBC News can project. If one party were to win both of these districts early in the night, that party could very well end up with the majority.

articles.title: Alaska voter 'disgusted' by reported 'decoy Dan' plot switches from Peltola to Sullivan
articles.summary: An Alaska voter who considered voting for former Rep. Mary Peltola, said he "switched" and would vote for incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
articles.body: As the Senate race in Alaska makes headlines over an alleged Democrat-linked election scheme, Fox News spoke with voters heading to the polls on Monday, including one man who said he is voting for incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, despite having previously considered voting for the Democratic Senate candidate, former Rep. Mary Peltola. The Senate race, which is a ranked-choice voting contest, has been the subject of significant national attention due to the inclusion of a candidate with nearly the same name as the incumbent GOP lawmaker. The male voter, who did not provide his name, explained that he "thought it was sketchy from the get-go." A New York Times report published last week detailed the alleged scam that involved Democrats seeking to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run in the race against the incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan. "When The New York Times article came out, and I found out how that transpired, I was disgusted by the whole thing, so sleazy," the voter noted. ELECTION DAY 2026: VOTERS CAST BALLOTS WITH CONTROL OF CONGRESS ON THE LINE A woman who was with the man in Alaska noted that he had "thought about voting for Mary Peltola." "I switched," he said. The woman said she believes it is "unethical, and I don't think [Peltola] should be elected." The man agreed. They both confirmed they would be voting for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. DOJ FACES 'HEAVY LIFT' IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES The Peltola campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday. In a rally speech last week, Peltola denied being involved in the alleged scheme. "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said. "I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan." Sen. Sullivan said during a speech on Monday, "We all knew that the decoy Dan guy was fake, but the extent of the corruption, the extent of the cheating."
